Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 1–5:

﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾

Explanation of the word:

Alif-Lam-Mim: These are among the disjoined letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a). They are written Alif-Lam-Mim and recited thus: "Alif, Lam, Mim." The surahs that open with disjoined letters number twenty-nine; the first of them is this surah (al-Baqarah) and the last is al-Qalam, "Nun." Among them are the single-letter ones, such as Sad, Qaf and Nun; the two-letter ones, such as Ta-Ha, Ya-Sin and Ha-Mim; and the three-, four- and five-letter ones. Nothing has been reliably transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ concerning their interpretation. That they belong to the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters whose knowledge God alone possesses is closer to the truth, and therefore it is said of them: "Alif-Lam-Mim: God knows best what He means by them."

Some scholars have drawn two benefits from them. The first: since the polytheists used to prevent people from listening to the Qur'an, lest it affect the hearts of the listeners, the utterance of these letters—Ha-Mim, Ta-Sin, Qaf, Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad—is a strange form of speech to them that draws them toward listening to the Qur'an; they listen, are affected, are attracted, and believe. And one benefit suffices for that. The second: when the polytheists denied that the Qur'an is the speech of God, revealed by Him to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, these letters served as a challenge to them, as if they were saying: "This Qur'an is composed of letters like these; so compose something like it yourselves." This benefit is supported by the fact that the word "Qur'an" mostly follows them, as in ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book﴾ and ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Book﴾ [Yunus: 1; Yusuf: 1; al-Hijr: 1], and ﴿Ta-Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾ [al-Naml: 1], as if they were saying: "The Qur'an is composed of letters such as these; so produce its like. If you are unable, then acknowledge that it is the speech of God and His revelation, and believe in it, and you will prosper."

﴿That is the Book, in which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing﴾

Explanation of the words:

That (dhalika): "this." The expression "that" was used instead of "this" because the distance-marker (lam of distance) conveys the lofty rank and elevated station of the Qur'an.

The Book (al-Kitab): the noble Qur'an which the Messenger of God ﷺ recited to the people.

No doubt (la rayba): there is no doubt that it is the revelation of God and His speech, which He revealed to His Messenger.

In it is guidance (fihi huda): a guide to the path that leads to happiness and perfection in both abodes.

For the God-fearing (lil-muttaqin): the muttaqin are those who guard themselves against God's punishment by obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

Meaning of the verse:

God informs that what He sent down upon His servant and Messenger, the Qur'an, is a Book, grand and magnificent, which admits no doubt, and no possibility that it is other than the revelation and Book of God in any way. That is because of its inimitability, and because of the guidance and light it carries for the people of faith and piety, by which they are guided to the paths of peace, happiness and perfection.

Guidance of the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse:

1. Strengthening faith in God, His Book and His Messenger, and urging the seeking of guidance from the noble Book.
2. Explaining the virtue of piety and its people.

﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them;

and those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and who are certain of the Hereafter.

Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾

Explanation of the phrases:

Who believe in the unseen (yu'minuna bil-ghayb): they affirm with firm conviction everything that is unseen and not perceived by the senses, such as the Lord, blessed and exalted, in His essence and attributes; the angels; the resurrection; Paradise and its bliss; and Hell and its punishment.

Establish the prayer (yuqimuna al-salat): they keep up performing the five daily prayers at their times, observing their conditions, pillars, sunnahs and the regular and other voluntary prayers.

Spend out of what We have provided for them (wa mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun): they spend some of the wealth God has given them, by paying the zakat on their wealth, by spending on themselves, their spouses, their children and their parents, and by giving charity to the poor and needy.

Believe in what has been sent down to you (yu'minuna bima unzila ilayka): they affirm the revelation sent down to you, O Messenger, which is the Book and the Sunnah.

And what was sent down before you (wa ma unzila min qablika): and they affirm what God sent down of Books to the messengers before you, such as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms.

And are certain of the Hereafter (wa bil-akhirati hum yuqinun): and of life in the abode of the Hereafter and what is in it of reckoning, reward and punishment, they are knowing and certain; they doubt nothing of that and have no misgivings, because of the completeness of their faith and the greatness of their piety.

Those are upon guidance from their Lord (ula'ika 'ala huda min rabbihim): the reference is to the possessors of the five qualities mentioned above, and the statement that, by the guidance God has granted them toward faith and righteous deeds, they are able to remain steadfast upon the way of God, which leads them to success.

And those are the successful (wa ula'ika hum al-muflihun): the reference is to the possessors of complete guidance, and the statement that they are the successful, deserving of the triumph that is entry into Paradise after deliverance from the Fire.

Meaning of the verses:

God mentioned in these three verses the qualities of the God-fearing: belief in the unseen, establishing the prayer, paying zakat, believing in the Books God sent down, and believing in the Abode of the Hereafter. He informed that, for this reason, they are upon the fullest guidance from their Lord, and that they are the ones who triumph in this world through purity and tranquility, and in the Hereafter through entry into Paradise after deliverance from the Fire.

Guidance of the verses:

Among the guidance of the verses:

Calling the believers to, and encouraging them toward, adopting the qualities of the people of guidance and success, so that they may follow their way, be guided, and prosper in this world and the next.

Who believe in the unseen (yu'minuna bil-ghayb): they affirm with firm conviction everything that is unseen and not perceived by the senses, such as the Lord, blessed and exalted, in His essence and attributes; the angels; the resurrection; Paradise and its bliss; and Hell and its punishment.

Establish the prayer (yuqimuna al-salat): they keep up performing the five daily prayers at their times, observing their conditions, pillars, sunnahs and the regular and other voluntary prayers.

Spend out of what We have provided for them (wa mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun): they spend some of the wealth God has given them, by paying the zakat on their wealth, by spending on themselves, their spouses, their children and their parents, and by giving charity to the poor and needy.

Believe in what has been sent down to you (yu'minuna bima unzila ilayka): they affirm the revelation sent down to you, O Messenger, which is the Book and the Sunnah.

And what was sent down before you (wa ma unzila min qablika): and they affirm what God sent down of Books to the messengers before you, such as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms.

And are certain of the Hereafter (wa bil-akhirati hum yuqinun): and of life in the abode of the Hereafter and what is in it of reckoning, reward and punishment, they are knowing and certain; they doubt nothing of that and have no misgivings, because of the completeness of their faith and the greatness of their piety.

Those are upon guidance from their Lord (ula'ika 'ala huda min rabbihim): the reference is to the possessors of the five qualities mentioned above, and the statement that, by the guidance God has granted them toward faith and righteous deeds, they are able to remain steadfast upon the way of God, which leads them to success.

And those are the successful (wa ula'ika hum al-muflihun): the reference is to the possessors of complete guidance, and the statement that they are the successful, deserving of the triumph that is entry into Paradise after deliverance from the Fire.

Meaning of the verses:

God mentioned in these three verses the qualities of the God-fearing: belief in the unseen, establishing the prayer, paying zakat, believing in the Books God sent down, and believing in the Abode of the Hereafter. He informed that, for this reason, they are upon the fullest guidance from their Lord, and that they are the ones who triumph in this world through purity and tranquility, and in the Hereafter through entry into Paradise after deliverance from the Fire.

Guidance of the verses:

Among the guidance of the verses:

Calling the believers to, and encouraging them toward, adopting the qualities of the people of guidance and success, so that they may follow their way, be guided, and prosper in this world and the next.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 6–7:

Explanation of the words:

Kafaru (disbelieved): Kufr (disbelief) linguistically means covering and denial; in the sacred law it means denying Allah and what His messengers brought from Him, entirely or in part.

Sawa'un (equal): meaning equal in regard to their being warned and not being warned, since there is no benefit in it, given Allah's judgment that they will not be guided.

A-andhartahum (did you warn them): Indhar (warning) means frightening [people] with the consequence of disbelief, wrongdoing and corruption.

Khatama Allah (Allah has sealed): it means stamped, for khatm (sealing) and tab' (stamping) are one and the same, namely placing a seal or stamp upon a container so that what is in it cannot be known and cannot be reached, so that it is not altered or changed.

Al-ghishawah (the covering): a cover with which what is intended to be prevented from reaching something is veiled.

Al-adhab (the punishment): pain that increases the sweetness and pleasure of life.

The relation of the two verses to what precedes them and their meaning:

When [Allah] mentioned the people of faith, piety, guidance and success, He then mentioned after them the people of disbelief, misguidance and loss, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ and so on. He informed [us] that they are not prepared for faith, such that warning them and not warning them is equal to them. This is due to the continuation of Allah's way regarding them: sealing their hearts so that they do not understand, and their ears so that they do not hear, and placing a covering over their eyes so that they do not see. This is the result of their obstinacy, their stubbornness and their persistence in disbelief. By this they deserved the great punishment, and it was decreed against them. This is Allah the Exalted's judgment concerning the people of stubbornness, obstinacy and persistence in every time and place.

Guidance from the two verses:

1- Clarification of Allah the Exalted's way regarding the people of stubbornness, obstinacy and persistence: that Allah deprives them of guidance by disabling their senses so that they do not benefit from them, and so they do not believe and are not guided.

2- A warning against persisting in disbelief, wrongdoing and corruption, which necessitates the great punishment.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 8–10:

Explanation of the words:

ومن الناس (Wa min an-nas): from among the people, i.e., from some of the people.

من يقول آمنا بالله (Man yaqulu amanna billah): "those who say, 'We believe in Allah'": we affirm belief in Allah as the one God, having no god besides Him and no lord other than Him.

وباليوم الآخر (Wa bil-yawm al-akhir): and in the Last Day: we affirm the resurrection and recompense on the Day of Judgment.

يخادعون الله (Yukhadi'unallah): they deceive Allah, by displaying belief and concealing disbelief.

وما يخدعون الا أنفسهم (Wa ma yakhda'una illa anfusahum): and they deceive none but themselves, since the consequence of their deception returns to them, not to Allah, nor to His Messenger, nor to the believers.

وما يشعرون (Wa ma yash'urun): and they are not aware, i.e., they do not know that the consequence of their deception returns to them.

في قلوبهم مرض (Fi qulubihim marad): in their hearts is a disease, i.e., doubt, hypocrisy, and the pain of fear of having their affair exposed and of being brought to account.

فزادهم الله مرضا (Fa zadahumullahu marada): so Allah increased them in disease: in doubt, hypocrisy, pain, and fear, in accordance with the sunnah (established way) of Allah that an evil deed brings about nothing but another evil deed.

عذاب أليم (Adhabun alim): a painful punishment, severe and grievous in its effect upon the soul.

Occasion of the verse in relation to what precedes it, and explanation of its meaning:

When Allah mentioned the believers who are complete in their faith, and their counterparts, the disbelievers who have reached the furthest extent of disbelief, He mentioned the hypocrites, who are believers outwardly and disbelievers inwardly. They are worse than the disbelievers who have reached the utmost of disbelief.

Allah informed that a group of people, namely the hypocrites, claim belief with their tongues while concealing disbelief in their hearts. They deceive Allah and the believers through this hypocrisy. Since the consequence of their deception returns to them,

they were by that deceiving themselves and no one else, but they do not know this and are not aware of it.

Allah also informed that in their hearts is a disease, which is doubt, hypocrisy and fear, and that He increased them in disease as a punishment for them in this world, and threatened them with a painful punishment in the Hereafter because of their lying and disbelief.

Guidance from these verses:

Warning against lying, hypocrisy and deception, and that the consequence of deception returns upon its perpetrator, just as an evil deed produces nothing but a similar evil deed.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 11–13:

Explanation of the words:

Corruption on the earth (al-fasad fi al-ard): disbelief and committing sins therein.

Reform on the earth (al-islah fi al-ard): it comes through correct faith and righteous deeds, and abandoning polytheism and sins.

Do not perceive (la yash'urun): they do not know and are not aware.

The foolish (al-sufaha'): plural of safih, one who is light-minded, not good at conduct and planning.

Meaning of the verses:

He, exalted is He, informs about the hypocrites that when one of the believers says to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth by hypocrisy and by allying yourselves with the Jews and the disbelievers," they reply, "We are only reformers," in their own claim. So God, exalted is He, refuted this claim and established that they alone are the corrupters, not those whom they disparaged among the believers, but they do not know this because disbelief has taken hold of their hearts. He, exalted is He, also informs about them that when one of the believers says to them, "Be sincere in your faith, and believe as so-and-so and so-and-so believe, such as Abdullah ibn Salam," they reply, "Shall we believe as the foolish believe, those who have no right guidance and no insight?" So God, exalted is He, rejected their claim, affirmed foolishness for them, negated it from the sincere believers, and described them with ignorance and lack of knowledge.

Guidance from the verses:

1- The condemnation of false claims, which are mostly found only among the attributes of the hypocrites.

2- Reform on the earth comes through acting in obedience to God and His Messenger, and corruption on the earth comes through disobeying God and His Messenger (ﷺ).

3- Those who practice corruption on the earth always justify their corruption as reform and not as corruption.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 14–16:

Explanation of the Words

Laqu (لَقُوا): al-liqa' (meeting) and al-mulaqah (encounter) mean confronting someone face to face.

Amanu (آمنوا): Faith (iman) in the Shari'ah sense is affirming belief in God and in everything that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought from God. Its true adherents are the believers (al-mu'minun) in the full sense.

Khalau (خلوا): To be alone with something (al-khuluw bi-al-shay') is to be in privacy with it.

Shayatinahum (شياطينهم): The shaytan (devil) is everyone who is far from good and close to evil, who corrupts and does not reform, whether among humans or jinn. What is meant here are their leaders in evil and corruption.

Mustahzi'un (مستهزئون): Istihza' (mockery) is belittling and ridiculing a person.

Al-Tughyan (الطغيان): Exceeding the limit in a matter and going to excess in it.

Al-'Amah (العَمَه): For the heart, it is like blindness is for the eye: the failure to see, and the bewilderment and misguidance that result from it.

Ishtaraw (اشتروا): They exchanged guidance for misguidance, meaning they abandoned faith and took up disbelief.

Tijaratuhum (تجارتهم): Tijarah (trade) is putting forward capital to buy something that yields profit when sold. The hypocrites here put forward their capital, which is faith, to buy disbelief, hoping to gain honor and wealth in this world. They lost and did not profit, for they were humiliated, punished, and impoverished because of their disbelief.

Al-Muhtadi (المهتدي): One who travels a path that leads him, by a direct course, to what he wants in the shortest time and without hardship. The one who is astray (al-dall) is the opposite of the guided one: he travels a path without a direct aim, so it does not bring him to his goal, and he perishes before arriving.

Meaning of the Verses:

The verses continue to speak of the hypocrites and describe their conditions. God, exalted is He, informs us in the first verse that, because of their hypocrisy and wickedness, when they meet those who believe in a certain place, they tell them that they believe in God, the Messenger, and what he brought of the religion. But when they are alone with their leaders in sedition and misguidance, they blame them for what they claimed of faith, and say to them: "We are with you in your religion, and we never believed. We only displayed faith as mockery and derision of Muhammad and his companions."

In the second verse [15], He informs that He, exalted is He, mocks them in return, as requital in kind, and increases them, according to His custom that an evil deed begets an evil deed, in their transgression, so that their bewilderment and the turmoil of their souls and the misguidance of their minds increase. In the verse [16], He informs that those far off in misguidance have exchanged faith for disbelief and sincerity for hypocrisy, so their trade does not profit, and they are not guided to a path of gain or success.

Guidance from the Verses

1- Condemnation of the hypocrites and a warning against their conduct of meeting one group with one face and another group with a different face. In a hadith: "The worst of you is the one with two faces."

2- Among people are devils who call to disbelief and sins, command what is evil, and forbid what is good.

3- An explanation of God's retribution, and its descent upon His enemies, mighty and majestic is He.

In the second verse [15], He informs that He, exalted is He, mocks them in return, as requital in kind, and increases them, according to His custom that an evil deed begets an evil deed, in their transgression, so that their bewilderment and the turmoil of their souls and the misguidance of their minds increase. In the verse [16], He informs that those far off in misguidance have exchanged faith for disbelief and sincerity for hypocrisy, so their trade does not profit, and they are not guided to a path of gain or success.

Guidance from the Verses

1- Condemnation of the hypocrites and a warning against their conduct of meeting one group with one face and another group with a different face. In a hadith: "The worst of you is the one with two faces."

2- Among people are devils who call to disbelief and sins, command what is evil, and forbid what is good.

3- An explanation of God's retribution, and its descent upon His enemies, mighty and majestic is He.

**Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on Surah 2, verses 17–20:**

**Explanation of the words:**

*Mathaluhum* (their likeness): their state and condition.

*Istawqada* (kindled): he lit a fire.

*Summun, bukmun, 'umyun* (deaf, dumb, blind): they neither hear, nor speak, nor see.

*Sayyib* (rain-cloud): rain.

*Zulumat* (darknesses): the darkness of night, the darkness of the clouds, and the darkness of the rain.

*Ra'd* (thunder): the crashing sound heard when the clouds gather and rain falls.

*Barq* (lightning): the light that flashes when the clouds gather and rain falls.

*Sawa'iq* (thunderbolts), plural of *sa'iqah*: a mighty fire that descends during the crashing of thunder and the flashing of lightning, with which Allah strikes whomever He wills.

*Hadhar al-mawt* (for fear of death): to guard against death.

*Muhit* (encompassing): that which surrounds a thing from all its sides.

*Yakad* (nearly): comes close to.

*Yakhtafu* (snatches): takes it swiftly.

*Absarahum* (their sights): plural of *basar*, meaning the seeing eye.

**Meaning of the verses:**

The likeness of these hypocrites, in what they show of faith while concealing unbelief, is like that of one who kindled a fire to benefit from its light. When it lit up what was around them and they gained from it the least benefit, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness where they cannot see. For by their outward faith they preserved their blood, their wealth, their women and their children from killing and captivity, while by the unbelief they harbour, if they die upon it, they will enter the Fire, and so they lose everything, even themselves. This parable is contained in the first verse [17]. As for the second verse [18], it is a report about those hypocrites that they have lost every readiness for guidance: their ears do not hear the voice of truth, their tongues do not speak it, and their eyes do not see its signs. This is because of their deep immersion in corruption, so they will not return from unbelief to faith in any state whatsoever.

As for the third and fourth verses [19] [20], they contain another parable for these hypocrites. The image, wondrous and fitting for their condition, is of heavy rain in darkness, accompanied by crashing thunder and flashing lightning, and they are in its midst, terrified and fearful, stopping their ears with their fingertips so as not to hear the sound of the thunderbolts, for fear that their hearts will be torn away and they die. They find no escape or refuge, because Allah encompasses them. On the other hand, the lightning, because of its intensity and speed, nearly snatches away their sight so that they become blind. When the lightning lights the way for them, they walk in its light; and when the lightning's light goes out, they stand bewildered and afraid. Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight, for He is over all things Powerful. This is the condition of those hypocrites. The Qur'an descends mentioning unbelief, which is darkness; mentioning the threat, which is like the thunderbolts and thunder; and with proofs and clear evidences, which are like the lightning in the strength of their illumination. They fear that the Qur'an will descend to expose them and lift the veil from them, so that they will be seized. Thus, when it descends with a verse that does not point to them or target them, they walk on in their outward faith. But when it descends with verses condemning their falsehood and what they are upon, they stand perplexed, neither advancing nor retreating. Had Allah willed to take away their hearing and sight, He would have done so, for they deserve that, and He is over all things Powerful.

**Guidance from these verses:**

From the guidance of these verses:

1. The commendability of coining parables to bring meanings closer to the minds.
2. The failure of the efforts of the people of falsehood and the evil outcome of their affair.
3. The Qur'an is the means by which hearts are revived, just as the earth is revived by rainwater.
4. The worst of the disbelievers are the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 21–22:

Explanation of the words:

Al-nas (the people): a plural noun with no singular form derived from its own root; its singular is insan (human being).

U'budu (worship): obey, through faith and by complying with the commands and prohibitions, together with the utmost love of God and reverence for Him.

Rabbukum (your Lord): your Creator, the Owner of your affairs, and your true God.

Khalaqakum (created you): brought you into existence from non-existence, with a great measure of design.

Tattaqun (that you may attain piety): that you take a shield that guards you from God, which is achieved through faith and righteous action after abandoning polytheism and sins.

Firasha (a bed): a resting place on which to sit and sleep upon.

Binaan (a canopy): a structure raised above you, like a dome.

Al-thamarat (the fruits): the plural of thamara, meaning what the earth produces of grains and greens, and what trees produce of fruits.

Rizqan lakum (provision for you): sustenance for you, by which you feed yourselves, so that your lives are preserved until their appointed term.

Andadan (equals): the plural of nidd, meaning a counterpart or likeness, which you worship besides God or alongside God, thereby setting up rivals to the Lord, blessed and exalted.

The occasion of revelation and the meaning of the two verses:

The connection is that when God mentioned the believers who prosper and the disbelievers who lose, He then mentioned the hypocrites, who stand between the sincere believers and the lost disbelievers. Then, in a shift of address, He called out to all of them with the title "people," so that it would be a general call to all of humanity in every place and time, and commanded them to worship Him so that they would protect themselves from loss. He made Himself known to them so that they might know Him by His attributes of majesty and perfection, which would be more compelling for them to respond, so they would worship Him in a way that saves them from His punishment and wins His pleasure and Paradise. He concluded His call by warning them against taking partners with Him whom they worship alongside Him, while knowing that these partners do not deserve worship because they are unable to benefit or harm them.

Guidance of the two verses:

From the guidance of the two verses:

1- The obligation to worship God, the Exalted, since it is the purpose of all life.

2- The obligation to know God through His names and attributes.

3- The prohibition of associating partners with God, both minor and major, apparent and hidden.

**Explanation of the Vocabulary**

**Al-rayb** (doubt): doubt accompanied by unease and disquiet of the soul.

**Abdina** (Our servant): Muhammad (ﷺ).

**Min mithlihi** (like it): like the Qur'an, or like Muhammad in being unlettered.

**Shuhadaakum** (your helpers): your supporters. It also means your deities, which you claim will testify for you before God and intercede for you.

**Waquduha** (its fuel): that with which it is kindled and set aflame, namely the disbelievers and the idols worshipped besides God, the Mighty and Majestic.

**U'iddat** (prepared): readied and made ready.

**Al-kafirin** (the disbelievers): those who deny the right of God, the Exalted, to be worshipped alone, and who reject His Messenger and His law.

**The Occasion and Meaning of the Verse**

When God, the Exalted, established in the previous verse the foundation of religion, which is tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), that He alone is to be worshipped, He establishes in this verse the second foundation of religion, which is the prophethood of His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). He does so by way of proof: if you are in doubt about the Qur'an that We have sent down upon Our servant and Our Messenger Muhammad, then produce a surah like its surahs, or [produce it] from an unlettered man like Our servant in his being unlettered. But if you fail to do so, because of your incapacity, then protect yourselves from the Fire by believing in the divine revelation and by worshipping God, the Exalted, in the manner He has prescribed.

**Lessons from the Verse**

1. Affirming the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by establishing that the Qur'an was sent down to him.

2. The incapacity of human beings to produce a surah like the surahs of the noble Qur'an is confirmed, even after the passing of one thousand four hundred and six years, while the challenge still stands. They have not produced a surah like the surahs of the Qur'an, because of His saying, ﴿and you will never do it﴾.

3. The Fire is averted by faith and righteous deeds. In the authentic hadith: "Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date."

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 25:

Explanation of the words:

Bashshara (to give good news): tabshir (giving good news) is informing someone of something that delights them, and this is usually something beloved to the soul.

Tajri min tahtiha (flow beneath them): the rivers flow through their trees and palaces. The rivers are rivers of water, rivers of milk, rivers of wine, and rivers of honey.

Wa-utu bihi mutashabihan (they will be given fruit that resembles one another): they are given fruits, and a dish is brought to them that resembles one another in color but differs in taste.

Mutahharah (purified): from menstrual blood, postnatal bleeding, and all other defects and imperfections.

Khalidun (abiding): they remain therein and never leave it.

Occasion and meaning:

When Allah the Exalted mentioned the Fire and its people, it was fitting to mention the Garden and its people, so that both warning (tarhib) and encouragement (targhib) would be complete, and these two are the instruments of guidance and reform.

In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted commands His Messenger to give good news to the believers who are upright, of the gardens that He has provided for them, beneath which rivers flow, and in which there are for them spouses purified and pure from every harm and filth, and they abide therein. He also informs us that when various kinds of fruit are brought to them, they will say: "This is what we were provided with before," in the world. He, the Exalted, also informs us that they are given it resembling in color but different in taste, as an increase in its goodness, its perfection, and the great pleasure taken in it.

Guidance of the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse:

1- The virtue of faith and righteous deeds, for by them the bliss mentioned in the verse belongs to those who possess them.

2- Encouraging the believers toward the Abode of Peace and the everlasting bliss within it, so that they may increase in desire for them and in working for them.

By doing good deeds and abandoning evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 26–27:

Explanation of the words:

*La yastahyi* (لا يستحيي): Shyness does not prevent Him from setting forth examples, even small ones such as a mosquito or something smaller than it, like its wing.

*An yadriba mathalan* (أن يضرب مثلاً): to make one thing an example (mathal) for another, which reveals its attribute and state, whether in ugliness or in beauty.

*Ma ba'udatan* (ما بعوضة): *ma* here is indefinite, meaning "a thing," i.e. whatever thing, that He makes an example; or it is an extra particle (za'ida). *Ba'udatan* is the second object. Ba'ud (بعوض) is the plural of ba'udah (بعوضة), which is the young of the bug (al-biqq).

*Al-haqq* (الحق): that which is necessarily established, such that the intellect deems its non-existence impossible.

*Al-fasiqun* (الفاسقون): fisq (فسق) is going out of obedience. The fasiqun are those who abandon God's command to have faith and to do righteous deeds, and who abandon shirk and sins.

*Yanqudun* (ينقضون): naqd (نقض) is undoing something after it has been firmly tied.

*Ahd Allah* (عهد الله): what God has enjoined upon people of faith and obedience to Him and to His Messenger ﷺ.

*Min ba'di mithaqihi* (من بعد ميثاقه): after its ratification and confirmation by oath or by calling witnesses to it.

*Yaqta'una ma amara Allahu bihi an yuwsal* (يقطعون ما أمر الله به أن يوصل): from sustaining faith, monotheism and obedience, and from maintaining the ties of kinship.

*Yufsidun fi al-ardh* (يفسدون في الأرض): corruption on earth occurs through disbelief and committing sins.

*Al-khasirun* (الخاسرون): those who are complete in loss, in that they lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.

Occasion of revelation and meanings

When God set forth the two earlier examples, the fire and the water, the hypocrites said: "God is too exalted and too majestic to set forth such an example." So God revealed, in refutation of them, His saying ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to set forth an example﴾, the verse.

4. A warning against fisq and what follows from it: breaking the covenant, severing good, and withholding what is right.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 26–27:

Explanation of the words:

*La yastahyi* (لا يستحيي): Shyness does not prevent Him from setting forth examples, even small ones such as a mosquito or something smaller than it, like its wing.

*An yadriba mathalan* (أن يضرب مثلاً): to make one thing an example (mathal) for another, which reveals its attribute and state, whether in ugliness or in beauty.

*Ma ba'udatan* (ما بعوضة): *ma* here is indefinite, meaning "a thing," i.e. whatever thing, that He makes an example; or it is an extra particle (za'ida). *Ba'udatan* is the second object. Ba'ud (بعوض) is the plural of ba'udah (بعوضة), which is the young of the bug (al-biqq).

*Al-haqq* (الحق): that which is necessarily established, such that the intellect deems its non-existence impossible.

*Al-fasiqun* (الفاسقون): fisq (فسق) is going out of obedience. The fasiqun are those who abandon God's command to have faith and to do righteous deeds, and who abandon shirk and sins.

*Yanqudun* (ينقضون): naqd (نقض) is undoing something after it has been firmly tied.

*Ahd Allah* (عهد الله): what God has enjoined upon people of faith and obedience to Him and to His Messenger ﷺ.

*Min ba'di mithaqihi* (من بعد ميثاقه): after its ratification and confirmation by oath or by calling witnesses to it.

*Yaqta'una ma amara Allahu bihi an yuwsal* (يقطعون ما أمر الله به أن يوصل): from sustaining faith, monotheism and obedience, and from maintaining the ties of kinship.

*Yufsidun fi al-ardh* (يفسدون في الأرض): corruption on earth occurs through disbelief and committing sins.

*Al-khasirun* (الخاسرون): those who are complete in loss, in that they lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 28–29:

Explanation of the words:

"How can you disbelieve in Allah": The interrogative here expresses amazement, along with rebuke and reproach, since there is no cause that would necessitate disbelief.

"And you were dead and He gave you life": This is a proof of the falsehood of their disbelief, for how can a servant disbelieve in his Lord when it is He who created him after he was not a thing.

"Then He causes you to die, then He brings you to life": Causing the living to die and bringing the dead to life both indicate the existence of the Lord, may He be exalted, and His power.

"Then to Him you will be returned": He means after the second life, which is the Resurrection of the Last Day.

"He created for you all that is on the earth": That is, He brought into existence the good things of the earth, all of it for your sake, so that you may benefit from it in your life.

"Then He turned to the heaven": He rose and ascended over it, subduing it, and so it became seven heavens.

"And completed them": He perfected their creation as seven perfect heavens.

"And He is Knowing of all things": A statement that His knowledge encompasses all things, and an indication of His power, His knowledge, and the obligation to worship Him.

The meaning of the two verses:

The address continues to the disbelievers, who were previously described with the basest qualities and the worst conditions. He said to them, in the manner of a shift in address, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ and so on.

He mentioned some of the proofs of His existence and His generosity, by which disbelief in Him becomes among the most repugnant of matters, and its holder among the lowest of creatures and the worst in state and final outcome. Among the proofs of His existence is giving life after death and causing death after life. Among the proofs of His generosity and power is that He created for people all that is on the earth, since their lives depend on it, and He created the seven heavens. And with all of that, His knowledge encompasses all things, glorified is He; there is no god but Him and no lord other than Him.

Guidance from the two verses:

From the guidance of the two verses:

1- The denunciation of disbelief in Allah, may He be exalted.

2- Establishing proof of the existence of Allah, His power, and His mercy.

3- The permissibility of everything on the earth of food, drink, clothing, and mounts, except what the specific evidence from the Book or the Sunnah has prohibited, based on His saying: ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 30:

Explanation of the words:

Al-mala'ikah (the angels): the plural of malak (malak is also pronounced malak with the lightened form), and they are a creation from the unseen world. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that Allah the Exalted created them from light.

Al-khalifah (the vicegerent): one who succeeds another. What is meant here is Adam (peace be upon him).

Yufsidu fiha (they will cause corruption in it): corruption on the earth occurs through disbelief and committing sins.

Yasfiku (they will shed): spilling blood by killing and wounding.

Nusabbihu bihamdika (we glorify You with Your praise): we say "Subhan Allah wa bihamdih" (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him). Tasbih (glorification) is declaring Allah exempt from whatever is unbefitting to Him, the Exalted.

Wa-nuqaddisu laka (and we sanctify You): so we declare You exempt from whatever is unbefitting to You. Taqdis (sanctification) is purification and keeping far from what is not fitting. The lam in laka is additional, for the strengthening of the meaning, since the verb qaddasa is transitive by itself; it is said qaddasahu.

The meaning of the verse:

Allah the Exalted commands His Messenger to mention His saying to the angels: "Indeed I am placing in the earth a vicegerent," one who will succeed Him in executing His rulings on the earth. The angels, in apprehension, questioned whether this vicegerent might be one of those who shed blood and cause corruption on the earth through disbelief and sins, by analogy with a kind of jinn from whom what they feared had occurred.

So their Lord informed them that He knows of the wisdoms and interests what they do not know.

The purpose of this reminder is to increase the mention of the proofs indicating the existence of Allah the Exalted, His power, His knowledge, and His wisdom, which necessitate faith in Him and worship of Him alone, to the exclusion of others.

Guidance of the verse:

From the guidance of the verse:

1- Asking one who knows of one who does not know.

2- Not rebuking the questioner, and answering him or turning him away gently.

3- Knowledge of the beginning of creation.

4- The nobility and virtue of Adam.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 31–33:

Explanation of the words:

Adam: the Prophet of God, the father of mankind, peace be upon him.

Al-asma' (the names): the names of all genera, such as water, plants, animals, and humankind.

ʿaradahum (He presented them): He presented the named things before them. Since rational beings were among them, the masculine (rational) form was given precedence; otherwise it would have said ʿaradaha (them, for non-rational things).

Anbi'uni (Inform me): Tell me.

Ha'ula' (these): those presented to them from among all the creatures.

Subhanaka (Glory be to You): an declaration of Your transcendence and holiness.

Ghayb al-samawat (the unseen of the heavens): what is hidden from sight in the heavens and the earth.

Tubdun (you reveal): you make manifest, from their saying ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and so on.

Taktumun (you conceal): you keep inwardly and hide, meaning what Iblis harbored of disobedience to God's command and of not obeying Him.

Al-Hakim (the All-Wise): the Wise who places everything in its proper place, and who does nothing and leaves nothing undone except for a wisdom.

Meaning of the verses:

In the context of the manifestations of His power, knowledge, and wisdom which necessitate that He alone be worshipped, God, Exalted, informs that He taught Adam the names of all existing things. Then He presented the existing things to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful in your claim that you are the most honored of creatures and the most knowledgeable." They were unable to do so, and they openly acknowledged their admission of that, saying, "Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us." Then God, Exalted, said to Adam, "Inform them of the names of those creatures presented," and he informed them of their names one by one, down to the bowl and the small bowl. Here the nobility of Adam over them became manifest, and their Lord rebuked them with His saying: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing?﴾

Guidance of the verses:

From the guidance of the verses:

1- The demonstration of God's power, in that He taught Adam the names of all creatures, and so he learned them.

2- The nobility of knowledge and the excellence of the knowing over the ignorant.

3- The virtue of acknowledging one's incapacity and deficiency.

4- The permissibility of rebuking one who claims a claim for which he is not qualified.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 34:

Explanation of the words:

Uskudu (اسجدوا): Sujud (prostration) is placing the forehead and nose on the ground, though it may also be done by bowing the head without placing it on the ground, but with humility and submission.

Iblis (إبليس): It is said his name was al-Harith. When he became arrogant toward obeying Allah, Allah made him mublis, that is, He drove him to despair of every good, and transformed him into a shaytan (devil).

Aba (أبى): He refused and declined to prostrate to Adam.

Istakbara (استكبر): He magnified himself within his own soul, so arrogance and envy prevented him from obeying by prostrating to Adam.

Al-kafirin (الكافرين): Plural of kafir (disbeliever). One who denies Allah Most High, or denies any of His signs, or denies one of His messengers, or denies His obedience.

Meaning of the verse:

Allah Most High reminds His servants of His knowledge, wisdom and bounty upon them by His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam..."﴾ a prostration of greeting and honour. So they prostrated, except Iblis, who magnified himself within his soul and refused to prostrate, which is obedience to Allah and a greeting to Adam, out of arrogance and envy of Adam for his nobility. Thus, by his refusal to obey Allah, he was among the disbelievers, the defiantly disobedient to the command of Allah, a matter which necessitated his being driven to despair and expelled.

Guidance of the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse:

1- Reminding of Allah's bounty, which necessitates gratitude and encourages it.

2- Warning against arrogance and envy, as they were the cause of Iblis's being driven to despair, and of the Jews' refusal to accept Islam.

3- Affirming the enmity of Iblis, and alerting to the fact that he is an enemy whose enmity must always be upheld.

4- Alerting to the fact that some sins amount to disbelief or lead to disbelief.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 35–37:

Explanation of the words:

Raghadan (رغداً): a pleasant and abundant life; it is called raghad (رَغَد).

Al-shajarah (الشجرة): a tree from among the trees of Paradise. It is permissible that it be a grapevine, a fig tree, or something else. Since Allah the Exalted has not specified its type, one should not ask about it.

Al-zalimin (الظالمين): those who wronged themselves by committing what Allah the Exalted had forbidden.

Fa-azallahuma (فأزلهما): He caused them to slip into error, which is their disobedience to Allah the Exalted's prohibition to them of eating from the tree.

Mustaqarr (مستقر): al-mustaqarr is the place of settling and residence.

Ila hin (إلى حين): al-hin is time in general, which may be short or long, and what is meant by it is the end of life.

Fa-talaqqa Adam (فتلقى آدم): Adam took up the words that Allah the Exalted cast to him, the words of repentance.

Kalimat (كلمات): they are His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23].

Fa-tab 'alayhi (فتاب عليه): He granted him the ability to repent, so he repented and his repentance was accepted, for He is the Ever-Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful.

Meaning of the verses:

In the first verse [35], Allah the Exalted informs of His honoring of Adam and his wife Eve, when He permitted them His Garden to dwell in, eating of its bounties whatever they wished, except one tree; He forbade them to approach it and to eat of its fruit, so that they would not be among the wrongdoers.

In the second verse [36], Allah the Exalted informs that Satan caused Adam and his wife to fall into the sin, when he made the eating from the tree appealing to them, so they ate from it. Then their private parts became apparent to them, and they were no longer fit to remain in the Garden. So they were sent down to the earth together with their enemy Iblis, to live there, some of them enemies to others until the end of life.

In the third verse [37], Allah the Exalted informs that Adam received the words of repentance from his Lord, and they are: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. So they said them in repentance, and Allah accepted their repentance, for He is the Ever-Accepting, the Most Merciful.

Guidance of the verses:

From the guidance of these verses:

1- The honor of Adam and his descendants with their Lord, the Exalted.

2- The evil of disobedience and its effects in turning blessing into calamity.

3- The enmity of Satan toward man, and the obligation to know this in order to guard against his whispering.

4- The obligation of repentance from sin, which is seeking forgiveness after acknowledging the sin, abandoning it, and regretting having committed it.

In the second verse [36], Allah the Exalted informs that Satan caused Adam and his wife to fall into the sin, when he made the eating from the tree appealing to them, so they ate from it. Then their private parts became apparent to them, and they were no longer fit to remain in the Garden. So they were sent down to the earth together with their enemy Iblis, to live there, some of them enemies to others until the end of life.

In the third verse [37], Allah the Exalted informs that Adam received the words of repentance from his Lord, and they are: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. So they said them in repentance, and Allah accepted their repentance, for He is the Ever-Accepting, the Most Merciful.

Guidance of the verses:

From the guidance of these verses:

1- The honor of Adam and his descendants with their Lord, the Exalted.

2- The evil of disobedience and its effects in turning blessing into calamity.

3- The enmity of Satan toward man, and the obligation to know this in order to guard against his whispering.

4- The obligation of repentance from sin, which is seeking forgiveness after acknowledging the sin, abandoning it, and regretting having committed it.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 38–39:

Explanation of the words:

"Ihbitu minha jami'an" (Go down from it, all of you): Descend from the Garden (al-Jannah) to the earth, so that you may live on it as enemies to one another.

"Fa-imma ya'tiyannakum minni hudan" (Then, if there comes to you from Me guidance): If there comes to you from your Lord guidance, a law (shar') whose contents are contained in a Book (kitab) and which is made clear by a Messenger (rasul).

"Fa-man ittaba'a hada'ya" (Then whoever follows My guidance): He who acts upon My law, does not oppose it, and does not deviate from it.

"Fa-la khawfun 'alayhim wa la hum yahzanun" (there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve): This is the answer (jawab) to the conditional clause "fa-man ittaba'a hada'ya." Its meaning is that following guidance leads the servant to a state where he neither fears nor grieves, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

"Kafaru wa kadhdhabu" (who disbelieve and deny): Kafaru (disbelieved): they rejected the law of God; and kadhdhabu (denied) His Messenger.

"Ashab al-nar" (companions of the Fire): its people, who will never leave it, such that they will never come out of it.

The meaning of the two verses:

He, may He be exalted, informs that He commanded Adam, Eve, and Iblis to descend to the earth after the Devil whispered to them and they both ate from the tree. He informed them that if guidance comes to them from Him and they follow it and do not turn away from it, they will be safe and happy, so they will have no fear and no grief. And He threatened whoever disbelieves in Him and denies His Messenger, does not believe, and does not do righteous deeds, with eternal abiding in the Fire.

Guidance from the two verses:

From the guidance of the two verses:

1- Disobedience causes misery and deprivation.

2- Acting upon the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ) brings security and happiness, while turning away from them brings fear, grief, misery, and deprivation.

3- Disbelief and denial result in eternal abiding in the Fire for their possessor.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on Surah 2, verses 40–43:

Explanation of the words:

Banu Isra'il (the Children of Israel): Isra'il is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them, and his descendants are the Jews, because in their origins they trace back to the twelve sons of Ya'qub.

Ni'mah (favour): Here it is a noun of genus, meaning favours (ni'am). The favours of Allah the Exalted upon the Children of Israel are many, and their individual examples will pass by in the following Qur'anic verses.

Awfu bi-'ahdi (fulfil My covenant): Fulfilling a covenant (al-wafa' bil-'ahd) means completing it. The covenant of Allah upon them is that they make clear the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and believe in him.

Awf bi-'ahdikum (I will fulfil your covenant): I will complete for you your covenant by admitting you to Paradise, after honouring you in this world and granting you dignity in it.

Wa-iyya-ya farhabun (and fear Me alone): Fear Me and do not fear other than Me.

Amanu bima anzaltu (believe in what I have sent down): The Noble Qur'an.

Wa la tashtaru bi-ayati (and do not exchange My signs): Do not take a substitute for making the truth clear regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Thamanan qalilan (a small price): The fleeting enjoyments of the life of this world.

Wa-iyya-ya fattaqun (and be wary of Me alone): Be wary of Me alone in your concealing of the truth and your denial of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), lest I send down My punishment upon you.

Wa la talbisu al-haqqa bil-batil (and do not mix truth with falsehood): That is, do not mingle the truth with falsehood so that it is not known and acted upon. This is their saying: "Muhammad is a prophet, but he has been sent to the Arabs, not to the Children of Israel."

Warka'u ma'a al-raki'in (and bow with those who bow): Ruku' in the legal sense is bending the back in an extended and balanced posture, with both palms placed on the knees. What is meant here is submission to Allah and Islam before Him, the Mighty and Majestic.

Context of the verses and their meaning:

Since the context of the preceding verses concerned Adam and his honouring, the prostration of the angels to him, and Iblis's refusal out of arrogance and envy, and since this was known to the Jews because they are People of the Book, it was fitting that Allah the Exalted address the Children of Israel, reminding them of what is obligatory upon them of faith and steadfastness. He addressed them by the title of their descent from Isra'il, peace be upon him, and commanded and forbade them. He commanded them to remember His favour upon them, so that they would thank Him by obeying Him, by believing in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) and in the guidance he brought. He commanded them to fulfil the covenant taken from them, so that He would fulfil for them what He promised them. He commanded them to fear Him and not to fear any other of His creatures, and commanded them to believe in the Noble Qur'an, and not to be the first to disbelieve in it. He forbade them from taking a substitute for making clear the truth regarding faith in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), a small price from the enjoyments of the life of this world, commanded them to be wary of Him in that, and warned them that if they concealed the truth His punishment would descend upon them. He forbade them from mixing the truth with falsehood, to repel the truth and keep away from it, so that they would not believe in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) by establishing prayer, giving zakat, and submitting to Allah the Exalted by accepting Islam and entering it like the rest of the Muslims.

Guidance from these verses:

1- The obligation to mention favours in order to thank Allah the Exalted for them.

2- The obligation to fulfil covenants, especially what the servant has covenanted with his Lord the Exalted.

3- The obligation to make the truth clear and the prohibition of concealing it.

4- The prohibition of mixing truth with falsehood to mislead people and turn them away from it, such as the saying of the Jews: "Muhammad is a prophet, but only for the Arabs," so that the Jews would not believe in him.

**Explanation of the Words:**

**Al-birr** (righteousness, piety, the comprehensive term for all good): Here it means believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) and entering Islam.

**Al-nisyan** (forgetting): The opposite of remembrance. Here it means abandoning or neglecting.

**Tilawat al-kitab** (reciting the Book): Reading it. The Book here is the Torah that was in the hands of the Jews.

**Al-'aql** (reason, intellect): An inner faculty by which a person distinguishes between what benefits and what harms, and between the righteous and the corrupt.

**Al-isti'ana** (seeking help): Asking for aid to be able to speak and act.

**Al-sabr** (patience): Restraining the self from what it dislikes.

**Al-khushu'** (humble submissiveness): The presence of the heart and the stillness of the limbs. Here it means submission to God and obedience to His commands and prohibitions.

**Yazunnuna** (they think): Here it means "they are certain" (yuqinun).

**Mulaqu rabbihim** (those who will meet their Lord): Through death, and returning to Him on the Day of Resurrection.

**Meaning of the Two Verses:**

In the first verse [44], God, blessed and exalted is He, censures the scholars of the Children of Israel for commanding some of the Arabs to believe in Islam and its Prophet while neglecting themselves and not commanding their own souls to do so, even though they recite the Torah, in which the sending of the Prophet Muhammad and the command to believe in him and follow him are mentioned. He rebukes them, reproaching them with His words: "Do you not then reason?" For the person of reason hastens to good and then calls others to it.

In the second and third verses [45-46], God guides the Children of Israel to seek help through patience and prayer, so that they may be able to confront the truth and declare it, which is belief in Muhammad and entry into his religion. Then He informs them that this confrontation is difficult and burdensome for the soul, and that only those who are humble before their Lord and certain of meeting God and returning to Him are able to bear it.

**Guidance from the Verses:**

1. The ugliness of the conduct of one who commands others to do good but does not do it himself.

2. Sin is ugly, and its being committed by a scholar is even uglier.

3. The legitimacy of seeking help in difficult and arduous affairs through patience and prayer, for the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever a matter distressed him, would turn to prayer.

4. The virtue of humility before God and submission to Him, and of remembering death and returning to God for reckoning and recompense.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 47–48:

Explanation of the words:

O Children of Israel (ya bani Isra'il): The explanation of this phrase has already been given.

I have favored you over the worlds (faddaltukum 'ala al-'alamin): He granted them blessings, both religious and worldly, which He did not grant to any other people. This was in the time of Musa (peace be upon him) and during their periods of righteousness and uprightness.

Guard yourselves against a Day (ittaqu yawman): The "Day" here means the Day of Resurrection, as indicated by the description attached to it. Guarding oneself against it means guarding against the terrors and punishment that occur in it, and this is achieved through faith and righteous deeds.

No soul will avail another (la tajzi nafs): No soul will suffice in place of another soul in any way, so long as it is disbelieving.

Nor will intercession be accepted from it (wa la yuqbal minha shafa'ah): This disbelieving soul is the one for whom the intercession of intercessors will not benefit.

Nor will they be helped (wa la hum yunsarun): By having the punishment averted from them.

Allah the Exalted calls upon the Children of Israel, asking them to mention His blessings upon them so that they may give thanks for them by believing in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) and accepting what he brought of the true religion, which is Islam. 1- The obligation to mention blessings so that they may be thanked through praising Allah and obeying Him.

2- The obligation to guard against the punishment of the Day of Resurrection through faith and righteous deeds, after abandoning shirk and sins.

3- Affirmation that intercession does not belong to a disbelieving soul, and that ransom on the Day of Resurrection is never accepted.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 49–53:

Explanation of the words:

Al-najat (deliverance): rescue from destruction, like being rescued from drowning or from punishment.

Ali Fir'awn (the people of Pharaoh): the followers of Pharaoh. Pharaoh was the king of Egypt in the time of Musa (peace be upon him).

Yasumunakum su'a al-'adhab (they inflict upon you the worst torment): they inflict upon you the worst torment, which is its most severe and dreadful form, and make you taste it.

Yastahyuna nisa'akum (they spare your women): they leave off slaughtering the girls so that they grow up for service, and they slaughter the boys out of fear of them when they grow up.

Bala' 'azim (a great trial): a severe test and examination that cannot be borne.

Faraqna bikum al-bahr (We divided the sea for you): We made it into two parts, with dry land between them that had no water, so that you could traverse it and be saved. The sea is the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea).

Ittakhadhtum al-'ijl (you took the calf): a calf of gold, fashioned for them by al-Samiri, who called them to worship it, and most of them worshipped it. This happened during Musa's absence from them.

Al-shukr (gratitude): acknowledging a blessing by recognizing it, praising God Most High for it, and employing it in what pleases Him.

Al-kitab wa al-furqan (the Book and the Criterion): al-Kitab: the Torah; al-Furqan: the miracles by which God Most High distinguished truth from falsehood.

Tahtadun (you may be guided): to knowledge of the truth in all your affairs, both religious and worldly.

Meaning of the verses:

These five verses contain four great blessings that God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, which He commanded them to remember so that they would give thanks for them by believing in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) and his religion, Islam.

The first blessing: their deliverance from Pharaoh and his people, by rescuing them from their unjust rule and from the various forms of torment they were inflicting on them. Among these: slaughtering their male children and leaving the girls alive to be used as servants in their homes.

The second: the splitting of the sea for them and the drowning of their enemy after their rescue while they looked on.

The third: God's pardon for the greatest lapse they committed and the crime they perpetrated, which was taking a manufactured calf as a god and worshipping it. God Most High pardoned them and did not punish them, in order that they might give thanks to Him by worshipping Him alone, without any other.

The fourth: what He honoured their prophet Musa (peace be upon him) with, namely the Torah, in which there is guidance and light, and the miracles that nullified the falsehood of Pharaoh and established the true call that Musa (peace be upon him) brought.

These blessings are the content of the five verses. Knowing them gives a general understanding of the meanings of the verses, except for the sentence ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾ in the first verse, which states that the torment the Children of Israel suffered at the hands of Pharaoh and his chiefs was in fact a great test and trial from God for them. Likewise, the third verse mentions God's appointment with Musa after the Children of Israel's deliverance: forty nights, namely the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, in order that He give him the Torah to judge the Children of Israel by. During his absence, al-Samiri gathered the jewelry of the Children of Israel's women, made from it a calf, and called them to worship it, and they worshipped it, thereby deserving punishment, except that God graciously pardoned them so that they would give thanks.

Guidance from these verses:

1. Mentioning blessings prompts gratitude for them, and gratitude is the purpose of mentioning a blessing.

2. God Most High tests His servants for lofty wisdoms, so it is not permissible to object to God regarding what He tests His servants with.

3. Shirk is injustice, because it places worship in other than its proper place.

4. The sending of messengers and the revelation of books, with their wisdom, is for guiding people to knowledge of their Lord and the way of drawing near to Him, so that they worship Him, and thereby are perfected and find happiness in both lives.

**Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on Surah 2, Verses 54–57**

**Explanation of Key Words:**

**Zulm al-nafs** (wronging oneself): Corrupting it with the sin of a crime.

**Bi-ittikhadhikum al-'ijl** (by your taking the calf): By your making the calf, which al-Samiri fashioned from the ornaments of your women, into a god that you worshipped.

**Al-Bari'** (the Originator): The Creator, may He be exalted.

**Faqtulu anfusakum** (then kill yourselves): He commanded them that whoever among them had worshipped the calf be killed by those who had not worshipped it. This was made their repentance, and they carried it out, and He accepted their repentance.

**Naral-Laha jahratan** (that we may see God openly): That we may see Him with our own eyes.

**Al-sa'iqah** (the thunderbolt): A scorching fire like that which comes with clouds, rain, and thunder.

**Ba'athnakum** (We revived you): We brought you back to life after your death.

**Al-ghamam** (the clouds): Thin, white clouds.

**Al-mann wa al-salwa** (manna and quails): Al-mann is a sweet, sticky substance like honey; al-salwa is a bird known as al-sumani (quail).

**Al-tayyibat** (the good things): The lawful.

**Context and Meaning of the Verses:**

When God mentioned to the Jews the blessings He bestowed upon their forefathers, requiring them to give thanks for them by believing in His Messenger, He reminded them here of some of the sins of their forefathers, so that they might take warning and believe. He reminded them of the incident of their taking the calf as a god and worshipping it. This occurred after their deliverance from the people of Pharaoh, when Moses went off to commune with God and left Aaron as his deputy over them. Al-Samiri made for them a calf of gold and said, "This is your god and the god of Moses, so worship it." Most of them obeyed him and worshipped the calf, and by doing so they became apostates (murtaddin). So God made their repentance from their apostasy to be that whoever had not worshipped the calf should kill those who had worshipped it. They killed seventy thousand of them, and that was their repentance, and God accepted their repentance; indeed He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful.

He also reminded them of another incident: when they worshipped the calf and apostasy occurred, Moses, by God's command, chose from among them seventy men of their best who had not been implicated in the crime of worshipping the calf, and he took them to Mount Sinai so that they might offer an apology to their Lord, may He be glorified and exalted, for the worship of the calf by their brethren. When they arrived, they said to Moses, "Ask your Lord to let us hear His speech." So He let them hear His words: "Indeed I am God; there is no god but Me. I brought you out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, so worship Me and do not worship other than Me."

When Moses informed them that God had made their repentance to be by killing themselves, they said, "We will not believe you," meaning, "We will not follow you in what you have said regarding our repentance by killing some of us by others, until we see God openly." This was a great sin on their part, for it was a denial of their Messenger. So God became angry with them and sent down upon them a thunderbolt which destroyed them; they died one by one while they looked on. Then He revived them after a day and a night, so that they would give thanks by worshipping Him alone, without any other.

He also reminded them of another blessing, His honouring and favouring them by shading them with clouds and sending down manna and quails during the episode of the wandering (al-tih) in the desert of Sinai. In His words, ﴿وما ظَلَمُونا﴾ (They did not wrong Us), there is an indication that the trial of the wandering was a punishment for them for abandoning jihad and for their audacity toward their Prophet when they said to him: ﴿فَٱذْهَبْ أنتَ ورَبُّكَ فَقاتِلاۤ إنّا هاهُنا قاعِدُونَ﴾ (So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed we are sitting right here) [al-Ma'idah: 24]. He did not wrong them in the trial of the wandering, but they were the ones who wronged themselves.

**Guidance from the Verses:**

1. Worshipping other than God by a believer, while knowing that it is worship of other than God, is considered apostasy and polytheism on his part.

2. The legitimacy of fighting apostates. In the hadith: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," but only after he has been asked to repent.

3. The purpose of all life is to give thanks to God by worshipping Him alone.

4. Lawful things, among foods, drinks and others, are what God has made lawful, and unlawful things are what God, may He be exalted, has made unlawful.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 58–59:

Explanation of the words:

Al-qaryah (the town): the city of Jerusalem (al-Quds).

Raghadan: a wide, comfortable and pleasant livelihood.

Sujjadan: bowing low and humbly before God, in submission and in gratitude to God for their deliverance from the wandering (al-tih, the wandering in the desert).

Hittah: Hittah is a form (fi'lah) like raddah and haddah, from radadtu and haddadtu. He commanded them to say hittah, meaning "unburden us of our sins" (ihtutt 'annā khaṭāyānā). It is pronounced with a raised vowel (raf') as a predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated meaning being: our entering the gate prostrating is a hittah (an unburdening) for our sins.

Naghfir: We will erase and cover up.

Khatayakum: al-khatayā is the plural of khati'ah: the sin that a servant commits.

Fabaddala: they changed the word that was said to them; they were told to say it, which is hittah, but they said: "a grain in a hair" (ḥabbah fī sha'rah).

Rijzan: a plague, the pestilence.

Yafsuqun: they go out of the obedience of God and of His messenger sent to them, who was Joshua (Yusha', peace be upon him).

Meaning of the two verses:

The first verse [58] contains a reminder to the Jews of a great event that befell their forefathers, in which God's blessing upon the Children of Israel was manifest, a situation that calls for gratitude. When the period of wandering had ended, both Moses and Aaron had died, and their successor among the Children of Israel was Moses' young man, Joshua son of Nun. He led them against the Amalekites, and God granted them victory over the land of Jerusalem. God commanded them with a command of honour and favour, saying: "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance. And thank Me for this blessing by entering the gate of the city bowing low, saying: 'Our entering the gate prostrating is an unburdening for our sins, which we committed by refraining from jihad in the time of Moses and Aaron.' We will forgive you your sins and increase the reward of the good-doers among you."

The second verse [59] contains another event in which the true nature of the Jews' bad character and their great shamelessness became manifest, through their changing the action they were commanded to do and the word that was said to them. So they entered the gate crawling on their backsides, saying: "A grain in a barley-corn!!" Therefore God took vengeance upon them and sent down upon the wrongdoers among them a plague that destroyed a great number of people, as a recompense for their defiance of God's command. And what has been mentioned is an admonition for the Jews, if only they would take heed.

Guidance from the two verses:

1- Reminding the children of the days of their fathers for admonition and lesson.

2- Abandoning jihad when it is obligatory brings humiliation and loss upon the community.

3- A warning against the consequences of wrongdoing, defiance and rebellion against the commands of the Lawgiver.

4- The prohibition of interpreting the legal texts so as to take them out of the intent of the Lawgiver.

5- The virtue of excellence in speech and action.

**Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on Surah 2, verses 60–61:**

**Explanation of the words:**

**Istasqa (asked for water):** Musa asked Allah, Exalted is He, to provide them with *al-suqya*, meaning water for drinking and other uses.

**Bi-asaka al-hajar (with your staff, the rock):** Musa's staff, which was with him from the time he left the land of Madyan. It is said that it was from the trees of Paradise, which Adam descended with, but Allah knows best. The rock is a square-shaped stone of the *kaddan* type, soft like clay. It is said that it is the stone that ran off with Musa's garment in a well-known incident, but it is also said that it is one of the other stones. Allah knows best.

**Fa-infajarat (and there gushed forth):** *Al-infijar* means splitting open. *Fa-infajarat* means that springs burst forth from the staff.

**Mashrabahum (their drinking place):** The place where they drink.

**Rizq Allah (the provision of Allah):** What Allah provides His servants of all kinds of food.

**Wa-la ta'thaw (and do not commit corruption):** *Al-'athaya* and *al-'ithiyy* mean the greatest corruption. Its verb is *'athiya* (like *radiya*), *ya'thaa* (like *yardaa*), and *'athaa* (like *'adaa*), *ya'thu* (like *ya'du*).

**Mufsidin (causing corruption):** *Al-ifsad* means acting in disobedience to Allah and His Messenger in all areas of life.

**Al-baql (herbs):** Its plural is *al-buqul*, meaning all kinds of vegetables, such as carrots, mustard, potatoes, and the like.

**Al-qitha' (cucumbers):** Cucumbers, *al-khiyar*, and similar vegetables.

**Al-fum (garlic or wheat):** *Al-fum* is wheat. It is also said to mean garlic, because onion is mentioned after it.

**Atastabdilun (do you exchange):** *Al-istibdal* means giving up one thing and taking another in its place.

**Adna (lower):** Less good, less beneficial, and less useful, such as exchanging *al-manna wa al-salwa* (the manna and quail) for garlic and herbs.

**Misran (a city):** One of the cities. It is said that this was said to them while they were in the wilderness (*al-tih*), as a challenge and a rebuke, because they had refused to fight the tyrants, so they were afflicted with wandering in the wilderness and deprived of the good things of the city of Jerusalem and Palestine.

**Duribat 'alayhim al-dhilla (humiliation was imposed upon them):** It surrounded them and clung to them. *Al-dhilla* means abasement and contempt.

**Wa-al-maskana (and wretchedness):** *Al-maskana* means poverty and humiliation.

**Ba'u bi-ghadab (they returned with wrath):** They returned, after their long labor and great gains, with the wrath of Allah and His displeasure upon them. How evil is what they returned with.

**Dhalika bi-annahum (that is because they):** *Dhalika* refers to what befell them: the humiliation, the poverty, and the wrath. *Bi-annahum* means because of their disbelief, their killing of the prophets, and their disobedience. The *ba'* here is causative.

**Al-i'tida' (transgression):** Going beyond truth to falsehood, from what is right to what is wrong, and from justice to oppression.

**The meaning of the two verses:**

Allah, Exalted is He, reminds the Jews contemporary with the revelation of the Qur'an in the City of the Prophet (Madina) of His favors toward their forefathers and of His days (of mercy) toward them. In the first verse, number [60], He reminds them that when they were thirsty in the wilderness, Musa asked his Lord for water, and He gave them drink through a miraculous means, so that this would be a sign for them to uphold faith and obedience. This was that Musa, peace be upon him, struck the rock with his staff, and water gushed from it from twelve places. Each place became a spring from which one of their twelve tribes drank, so that they would not crowd one another and be harmed. Allah honored them with this blessing, and He forbade them from corrupting the earth by committing sins.

In the second verse [61], He reminds them of the bad characters that existed among their predecessors, including impatience, obstinacy, poor judgment, ignorance of what is good, recklessness, and others. This is evident in their saying, "O Musa," instead of "O Prophet of Allah" or "O Messenger of Allah," "We will not be patient with one kind of food," and their saying, "Ask your Lord for us," instead of "Ask Allah for us" or "Ask our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, for us." In their desires, they wanted meat and honey, and in place of them they asked for garlic and onions. Musa, peace be upon him, said, "Do you exchange what is lower for what is better?", which confirms this. He also reminded them of the bitter consequence that resulted from their disbelief in the signs of Allah, their killing of the prophets, their transgression, and their disobedience: Allah imposed humiliation and poverty upon them and became angry with them.

All of this, and what else Allah reminded the Jews of in His Book, is so that they might remember, be admonished, and be grateful, and then believe in His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), enter his religion, be perfected, and be happy, after being saved from what has befallen them of humiliation, poverty, and wrath in this world, and from the punishment of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection.

**Guidance from the two verses:**

1. The commendability of admonition and reminding people of the blessings and vengeance of Allah.
2. The obligation on the one who has received a blessing to thank for it, which is done by obeying Allah, performing His commands and abstaining from His prohibitions.
3. The condemnation of bad character and the denunciation of those who have it, as a lesson and an example.
4. The denunciation of major sins, such as disbelief and killing a soul without right, especially the killing of prophets or their successors, who are the scholars who enjoin justice in the community.
