Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 174–176:

Explanation of the words:

Yaktumun (يكتمون): they deny and conceal.

Ma anzala Allah mina al-kitab (ما أنزل الله من الكتاب): the Book is the Torah, and what God revealed in it concerning the description of the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and the command to believe in him.

La yukallimuhum Allah (لا يكلمهم الله): because of His wrath against them and His curse upon them.

Wa la yuzakkihim (ولا يزكيهم): He does not purify them from their sins, because He is not pleased with them.

Al-dalala (الضلالة): blindness that prevents guidance to the desired goal.

Al-shiqaq (الشقاق): dispute and enmity, such that its bearer is on one side and his opponent on the other.

Ba'id (بعيد): it is difficult to end, and reconciliation does not follow it.

Meaning of the verses:

These three verses were certainly revealed concerning the rabbis of the People of the Book, censuring their conduct and showing them the recompense for their concealing the truth and selling the knowledge which was taken from them to make clear, for a base worldly price. They deny the command and religion of the Prophet (ﷺ) to please the common folk, so that they will not cut off their gifts and financial support, and so that they retain their spiritual authority over them. This is the meaning of the words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price﴾. God the Most High also informed that what they eat of bribes in their bellies is nothing but fire, since it is what causes it, and with the fire is the anger of the Almighty; so He will not speak to them, nor purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.

As God the Most High informed about them in verse [175], they, being the distant ones, bought error in exchange for guidance, meaning disbelief in exchange for faith, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness, meaning the Fire in exchange for Paradise. How bold these people are against the disobedience of God and in plunging into the Fire! Therefore He said: ﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ All of this which has been completed is part of what God threatened these disbelievers with, because God sent down the Book with truth, clarifying in it the path of guidance and what it secures for its travellers of lasting bliss, and clarifying the path of misguidance and what it leads its travellers to of God's anger and His painful punishment.

In the last verse [176], God the Most High informed that those who differed concerning the Book, the Torah and the Gospel, namely the Jews and the Christians, are in enmity and difference between them that is far-reaching. God spoke truly, for the Jews and Christians have never ceased to be divided and hostile until today. The fruit of their disagreement concerning the truth which God sent down and commanded them to adhere to is that they abandoned it and took up falsehood, so it bore for them far-reaching dissension.

Guidance from the verses:

Among the guidance from the verses:

1- The prohibition of concealing the truth, especially when it is done to obtain worldly benefits, whether wealth or leadership.

2- A warning to the scholars of Islam against following the path of the scholars of the People of the Book in concealing the truth and issuing judgments to people based on falsehood in order to obtain specific material benefits.

3- A warning against disagreement concerning the Holy Qur'an, since it leads to enmity and far-reaching dissension among Muslims.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 177:

Explanation of the words:

Al-Birr (piety, righteousness): a term comprising every good and every act of obedience to Allah and His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ).

Wa-lakinna al-birra man amana billah (But righteousness is [in] the one who believes in Allah): true righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah and the Last Day, through to the end of the attributes.

Wa-ata al-mala ala hubbihi (And gives wealth despite loving it): he gives wealth where its giving is required, despite his strong love for it, preferring what Allah the Exalted loves over what he himself loves.

Dhawi al-qurba (the near of kin): the people of kinship, the nearest first, then the next nearest.

Al-yatama (orphans): plural of yatim (orphan), one whose father has died before he reached puberty (al-hunth).

Al-masakin (the needy): plural of miskin, a destitute poor person whom need has rendered unable to act freely.

Ibn al-sabil (the wayfarer): the traveller far from home, cut off from his family and his wealth.

Al-sa'ilin (those who ask): plural of sa'il, the poor person in need who is permitted to ask in order to relieve his own dire need.

Fi al-riqab (for the freeing of slaves): riqab is the plural of raqaba, and spending on them means spending on their emancipation.

Al-ba'sa'a wa al-darra' (adversity and affliction): al-ba'sa' is the severity of misery from poverty, and al-darra' is the severity of harm or sickness.

Wa-hina al-ba's (and in time of battle): at the time of fighting and its intensity in the cause of Allah the Exalted.

Ulaika alladhina sadaqu (those are the ones who are true): that is, in their claim of faith, righteousness and piety.

Explanation of the noble verse:

In the three verses preceding this one, Allah the Blessed and Exalted censured the rabbis of the People of the Book, mentioned the anger and painful punishment with which He threatened them on the Day of Resurrection, and this contained a warning to the scholars of Islam not to conceal knowledge from people in pursuit of the fleeting pleasures of this world. In this verse, Allah the Exalted also refuted the People of the Book for their boasting about the qibla and their claim of faith and perfection in it, merely because they pray towards their qibla, Bayt al-Maqdis, in the west, or towards the rising of the sun in the east. The first is the qibla of the Jews and the second is the qibla of the Christians. So Allah the Exalted said: "It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west." In this there is a great admonition to the Muslim who confines his Islam to prayer and does not care what obligations he neglects or what prohibitions he commits after it. Allah the Exalted then showed them the true righteous one in the claim of faith, Islam and excellence, saying: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾, that is, the one of righteousness, or the truly righteous one, is ﴿one who believes in Allah﴾, and He mentioned the pillars of faith except the sixth of them (qada' and qadar, divine decree). ﴿and establishes prayer and gives zakah﴾, and these two are among the greatest pillars of Islam. He spends wealth for the love of Allah despite his love for it and his attachment to it, to ﴿the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾, so he spends his wealth on those from whom he expects no reward, no praise and no thanks, such as the needy, the wayfarers and those who ask from among those in dire want and hunger. Freeing slaves and ransoming captives is also included. "Establishes prayer" means maintaining it and performing it in its most perfect form, and "gives zakah" means giving it to those entitled to it. Establishing prayer and giving zakah are among the greatest foundations of Islam. He also mentioned among their qualities fulfilling covenants and patience in the most difficult circumstances and severest conditions, saying: ﴿and those who fulfill their promise when they promise, and are patient in poverty and affliction and in time of battle﴾. This is the principle of ihsan, which is being mindful of Allah and seeing Him while performing worship. From here Allah the Exalted established that these are the truthful in their claim of faith and Islam, and they are the truly God-conscious who are protected from the anger of Allah and His painful punishment; may Allah make us among them. He said, indicating them with the particle of distance and the second-person pronoun, because of the elevation of their station and the height of their ranks: ﴿Those are the ones who are true, and those are the God-conscious.﴾

Guidance of the noble verse:

Among the guidance of the noble verse:

1- Being content with some matters of religion without carrying out others does not make its doer a believer or one who is saved.

2- The pillars of faith are those mentioned in this verse, and what is meant by "the Book" in the verse is the books.

3- Clarification of the avenues of spending whose reward is hoped for on the Day of Resurrection, namely the near of kin, etc.

4- Clarification of the great status of prayer and zakah.

5- The obligation of fulfilling covenants.

6- The obligation of patience, especially in battle.

7- Taqwa is the criterion of the matter, and the goal beyond which there is no goal for those who act.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 178–179:

Explanation of the words:

"Kutiba 'alaykumu al-qisas" (prescribed for you retribution): "kutiba" means "was made obligatory." "Al-qisas" (retaliation, the law of equal retribution) is when the next of kin of the victim does not accept blood-money and does not pardon.

"Fi al-qatla" (in the case of the slain): the "fa" here indicates causation, meaning because of the killing. "Al-qatla" is the plural of "qatil" (slain), the one whose soul has been taken, who has died by any means whatsoever.

"Al-hurr" (the free): the opposite of "al-abd" (the slave), and "al-abd" is the enslaved, the owned person.

"Fa man 'ufiya lahu min akhihi shay'" (but whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way): whoever the next of kin of the victim gives up retaliation for, in favour of blood-money or pardon.

"Fa-ittiba'un bi-ma'ruf" (then let there be due pursuit with fairness): it is obligatory that the demand for blood-money be made in a fair manner, with gentleness and kindness.

"Wa ada'un ilayhi bi-ihsan" (and payment made to him in good manner): that the payment of blood-money be made in a good manner, free from procrastination and shortfall.

"Dhalika takhfifun min rabbikum" (that is a lightening from your Lord): that is, that just and merciful ruling, namely the permissibility of accepting blood-money in place of retaliation, is a lightening from your Lord for you, since in the law before you there was only retaliation or only blood-money, whereas you have the choice between pardon, blood-money and retaliation.

"Fa man i'tada ba'da dhalika" (whoever transgresses after that): meaning one who takes blood-money and then kills; he is to be killed without exception.

"Al-qisas" (retaliation): equality in killing, in wounds, and also in the instrument of killing.

"Hayah" (life): a comprehensive, general preservation, for whoever intends to kill remembers that he will be killed and so refrains from killing, and thus the one he intended to kill lives, and by the life of both a great multitude of people lives.

"Ulu al-albab" (people of sound intellect): those with superior reason; the singular of "albab" is "lubb," which in a human being is the intellect.

"La'allakum tattaqun" (so that you may be mindful): that by this wise legislation He prepares you to guard against what harms and does not benefit, in this world and the next.

Meaning of the noble verses:

These verses were revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs, one of which regarded itself as nobler than the other, so it would kill a free man for a slave and a man for a woman, out of arrogance and pride. A killing then occurred between the two tribes while they were in Islam, so they complained of this to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and these verses were revealed, nullifying the blood-feud of the Jahiliyyah and establishing the principle of justice and equality in Islam. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retribution for those slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. Thus a free man is not to be killed for a man by two men, nor a woman by a man, nor a woman by two women, nor a free man for a slave by two slaves.

"Fa man tunazala lahu akhuhu" (whoever is pardoned by his brother, the next of kin): whoever the next of kin of the victim gives up retaliation for, in favour of blood-money or unconditional pardon, let him follow that and not say, "I will accept nothing but retaliation." Rather, he must accept what his brother has pardoned him of, whether retaliation, blood-money or pardon. The next of kin should demand the blood-money with gentleness and courtesy, and the killer should pay the blood-money in a good manner, without procrastination and without reducing any of it.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned His favour upon the Muslims in that He made this matter easy for them, making the next of kin free to choose among three: pardon, blood-money, or retaliation (qisas). Whereas the Jews were obligated only to retaliation, and the Christians only to blood-money. And He, exalted is He, informed of another ruling in this matter: that whoever takes blood-money and pardons the killing, then reverts and kills, ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾.

Scholars differed as to whether this painful punishment is the punishment of this world, by killing, or the punishment of the Hereafter. On this basis, Malik and al-Shafi'i said the ruling on this transgressor is the same as the ruling on the original killer: if pardoned, he is accepted; and if the retaliation or blood-money is demanded of him, it is given. Others said that the blood-money is returned by him and the matter is left to Allah's command. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, said that his case is referred to the imam, who rules in it in whatever way achieves the public interest.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that in the retaliation which He legislated for us and prescribed upon us, together with the lightening, there is great life, because it restrains the taking of souls and the shedding of blood. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And for you in retribution is life, O people of sound intellect, that you may be mindful﴾.

Guidance from the noble verses:

1. The ruling on retaliation in Islam is equality and parity: a man is killed for a man, a woman for a woman, a woman for a man, and a man for a woman, and the killer is killed by the same means with which he killed, in accordance with the hadith: "A person is killed for what he killed with." Since a slave is valued in property, he is not killed for a free man; rather, property is paid to his master. This was the ruling of the Companions and the Successors, and the three imams, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, hold it. Abu Hanifa differed, holding that retaliation applies, so a free man is killed for a slave, taking the apparent meaning of this verse.

2. The excellence of the Islamic law and what it contains of ease and mercy, in that it permits pardon and blood-money in place of retaliation.

3. The eloquence of the Noble Qur'an: the wise men of the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to say, "Killing is the best deterrent to killing," and the Qur'an said, ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾, without mentioning the word "killing" at all, thus negating it both verbally and in reality.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 178–179:

Explanation of the words:

"Kutiba 'alaykumu al-qisas" (prescribed for you retribution): "kutiba" means "was made obligatory." "Al-qisas" (retaliation, the law of equal retribution) is when the next of kin of the victim does not accept blood-money and does not pardon.

"Fi al-qatla" (in the case of the slain): the "fa" here indicates causation, meaning because of the killing. "Al-qatla" is the plural of "qatil" (slain), the one whose soul has been taken, who has died by any means whatsoever.

"Al-hurr" (the free): the opposite of "al-abd" (the slave), and "al-abd" is the enslaved, the owned person.

"Fa man 'ufiya lahu min akhihi shay'" (but whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way): whoever the next of kin of the victim gives up retaliation for, in favour of blood-money or pardon.

"Fa-ittiba'un bi-ma'ruf" (then let there be due pursuit with fairness): it is obligatory that the demand for blood-money be made in a fair manner, with gentleness and kindness.

"Wa ada'un ilayhi bi-ihsan" (and payment made to him in good manner): that the payment of blood-money be made in a good manner, free from procrastination and shortfall.

"Dhalika takhfifun min rabbikum" (that is a lightening from your Lord): that is, that just and merciful ruling, namely the permissibility of accepting blood-money in place of retaliation, is a lightening from your Lord for you, since in the law before you there was only retaliation or only blood-money, whereas you have the choice between pardon, blood-money and retaliation.

"Fa man i'tada ba'da dhalika" (whoever transgresses after that): meaning one who takes blood-money and then kills; he is to be killed without exception.

"Al-qisas" (retaliation): equality in killing, in wounds, and also in the instrument of killing.

"Hayah" (life): a comprehensive, general preservation, for whoever intends to kill remembers that he will be killed and so refrains from killing, and thus the one he intended to kill lives, and by the life of both a great multitude of people lives.

"Ulu al-albab" (people of sound intellect): those with superior reason; the singular of "albab" is "lubb," which in a human being is the intellect.

"La'allakum tattaqun" (so that you may be mindful): that by this wise legislation He prepares you to guard against what harms and does not benefit, in this world and the next.

Meaning of the noble verses:

These verses were revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs, one of which regarded itself as nobler than the other, so it would kill a free man for a slave and a man for a woman, out of arrogance and pride. A killing then occurred between the two tribes while they were in Islam, so they complained of this to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and these verses were revealed, nullifying the blood-feud of the Jahiliyyah and establishing the principle of justice and equality in Islam. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retribution for those slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. Thus a free man is not to be killed for a man by two men, nor a woman by a man, nor a woman by two women, nor a free man for a slave by two slaves.

"Fa man tunazala lahu akhuhu" (whoever is pardoned by his brother, the next of kin): whoever the next of kin of the victim gives up retaliation for, in favour of blood-money or unconditional pardon, let him follow that and not say, "I will accept nothing but retaliation." Rather, he must accept what his brother has pardoned him of, whether retaliation, blood-money or pardon. The next of kin should demand the blood-money with gentleness and courtesy, and the killer should pay the blood-money in a good manner, without procrastination and without reducing any of it.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned His favour upon the Muslims in that He made this matter easy for them, making the next of kin free to choose among three: pardon, blood-money, or retaliation (qisas). Whereas the Jews were obligated only to retaliation, and the Christians only to blood-money. And He, exalted is He, informed of another ruling in this matter: that whoever takes blood-money and pardons the killing, then reverts and kills, ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾.

Scholars differed as to whether this painful punishment is the punishment of this world, by killing, or the punishment of the Hereafter. On this basis, Malik and al-Shafi'i said the ruling on this transgressor is the same as the ruling on the original killer: if pardoned, he is accepted; and if the retaliation or blood-money is demanded of him, it is given. Others said that the blood-money is returned by him and the matter is left to Allah's command. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him, said that his case is referred to the imam, who rules in it in whatever way achieves the public interest.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that in the retaliation which He legislated for us and prescribed upon us, together with the lightening, there is great life, because it restrains the taking of souls and the shedding of blood. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And for you in retribution is life, O people of sound intellect, that you may be mindful﴾.

1. The ruling on retaliation in Islam is equality and parity: a man is killed for a man, a woman for a woman, a woman for a man, and a man for a woman, and the killer is killed by the same means with which he killed, in accordance with the hadith: "A person is killed for what he killed with." 2. The excellence of the Islamic law and what it contains of ease and mercy, in that it permits pardon and blood-money in place of retaliation.

3. The eloquence of the Noble Qur'an: the wise men of the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to say, "Killing is the best deterrent to killing," and the Qur'an said, ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾, without mentioning the word "killing" at all, thus negating it both verbally and in reality.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 180–182:

Explanation of the words:

Kutiba (كُتِبَ): was made obligatory and prescribed.

Khayran (خيراً): money in cash, goods, or real estate.

Al-wasiyyah (الوصية): the bequest, which is what is bequeathed from wealth and other things.

Al-ma'ruf (المعروف): what people customarily recognize, whether much or little, such that it does not exceed one-third.

Al-tabdil (التبديل): changing one thing for another.

Janafan aw ithman (جنفاً أو إثماً): janaf is deviation from the truth by error, and ithm is the deliberate departure from truth and justice.

The meaning of the verses:

In connection with the mention of the verse of retaliation (qisas), in which the killer is exposed to being killed and it is required of him that he make a bequest concerning his property before he is killed, the Exalted mentioned the verse of bequest, saying: "It is prescribed for you, O Muslims, that when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, a bequest be made to the parents and the near relatives according to what is customary; this is a duty upon the God-fearing." Then God abrogated this ruling by the verse of inheritance, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There is no bequest to an heir." The obligation was abrogated and the recommendation remained, but for those other than the parents and the heirs among the relatives. Unless the heirs permit it, and the bequest should be one-third or less. If it exceeds that and the heirs permit it, it is valid, based on the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Daraqutni: "A bequest to an heir is not valid unless the heirs wish it." The evidence for the recommendation of bequest is the hadith of Sa'd in the Sahih, where the Messenger permitted him to bequeath one-third. A bequest may also be obligatory upon a Muslim, if he leaves binding debts and obligatory rights upon him, so it is incumbent that he bequeath for their payment and collection after his death, based on the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in the Sahih: "No right of a Muslim man who has something to bequeath should pass two nights without his bequest being written and kept with him." This is what the first verse [180] contains. As for the second verse [181], God says to His believing servants: whoever alters a bequest made by a believer, by adding to this ruling or by changing it from one kind to another, then there is no sin on the testator, but the sin is upon the one who altered and changed it. He concluded this ruling with His saying: "Indeed God is Hearing and Knowing," as a warning and threat to whoever undertakes to change bequests for a corrupt purpose and evil desire. In the last verse [182], God informs that whoever fears from a testator janafan (deviation) or a leaning away from truth and justice, such as one who acts unjustly in his bequest without deliberately intending injustice but by error, or fears ithman (sin) on the testator, since he acted unjustly and transgressed knowingly in his bequest, and then reconciles between them, i.e., between the testator and the beneficiaries, there is no sin upon him in correcting the error and rectifying the mistake and oversight. He concluded this ruling with His saying: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, a promise of forgiveness and mercy for whoever errs without intent.

Guidance from the verses:

1- The abrogation of bequest to heirs absolutely, except with the permission of the heirs.

2- The recommendation of bequeathing wealth for one who leaves much property, to be spent in the paths of righteousness and goodness.

3- The emphasis of bequest, whether or not death is present, for one who has rights owed to him or owed by him, out of fear that he dies and the rights are lost, in which case he sins by their loss.

4- The prohibition of altering and changing a bequest to something other than what is righteous.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 183–184:

Explanation of the words:

kutiba (كُتِبَ): was made obligatory and prescribed.

al-Siyam (الصيام): linguistically means abstaining; here it means abstaining from eating, drinking and sexual relations from the break of dawn until sunset.

ayyaman ma'dudat (أياماً معدودات): twenty-nine or thirty days, according to the month of Ramadan.

fa'iddatun min ayyamin ukhar (فعدة من أيام أخر): so for whoever broke the fast due to the excuse of illness or travel, there is a obligation to fast other days equal in number to the days on which he broke his fast.

yutiqunahu (يطيقونه): that is, they bear it with hardship due to old age or an illness from which recovery is not expected.

fidyatun ta'amu miskin (فدية طعام مسكين): the obligation on one who breaks the fast for one of the aforementioned excuses is to feed one needy person for each day, and there is no qada' (making up) upon him.

fa man tatawwa'a khayran (فمن تطوع خيراً): that is, he who adds to the feeding, or feeds more than one needy person, it is better for him.

wa an tasumu khayrun lakum (وأن تصوموا خير لكم): fasting is better for the one who is able to do it, even with hardship, than breaking the fast with feeding.

Explanation of the two verses:

When the Messenger ﷺ migrated to Madinah and it became the abode of Islam, legislation began to descend and follow in succession. In the preceding verses there were the rulings on retaliation (qisas), bequest, and being mindful of Allah in these matters. Among the greatest qualities of taqwa that a believer can attain is fasting. So Allah the Exalted prescribed fasting in the second year after the Hijrah. He addressed them with the title of faith, "O you who believe," and informed them that fasting was prescribed for them just as it was prescribed for the nations before them. He said: ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you...﴾ and He gave the reason for it in His words: "so that you may have taqwa," meaning that He prepares them through it for taqwa, which is carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions, because of what fasting contains of being mindful of Allah the Exalted. His words ﴿ayyaman ma'dudat﴾ were mentioned to make the burden and hardship of fasting easier for them, since He did not make it months or years. He further lightened it by permitting the sick and the traveler to break the fast and make it up after recovery or return from travel. So He said to them: ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days.﴾ Likewise, one who is neither sick nor traveling but is able to fast only with severe hardship and difficulty may break the fast and feed one needy person for each day, and He informed them that fasting in this case is better. Then this last ruling was abrogated by His words in the next verse: ﴿So whoever witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ and His words ﴿if you knew﴾ mean: if you knew the benefits of fasting in this world and the Hereafter, which are many, the most important of which is the forgiveness of sins and the removal of diseases.

Guidance from the verses:

Among the guidance of these verses:

1- The obligation of fasting, which is the month of Ramadan.

2- Fasting cultivates the quality of taqwa in the believer.

3- Fasting expiates sins, based on the hadith: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." 

4- The concession to break the fast for the sick and the traveler.

5- The pregnant or nursing woman: the words "and for those who are able to do it" indicate that it is permissible for them to break the fast and make it up later; likewise the elderly person, who breaks the fast and does not make it up, and the one with an illness from which recovery is not expected, similarly. However, they must each feed one needy person for each day by giving him two handfuls of food. Likewise, if a pregnant or nursing woman fears for her child or her baby, or for herself, she must feed a needy person along with each fast she makes up.

6- Fasting has great religious and social benefits, alluded to by the phrase "if you knew."

Among these benefits:

1- The fasting person gains fear of Allah the Exalted, in private and in public.

2- It breaks the intensity of desire, which is why the unmarried person is directed to fasting.

3- It cultivates compassion and mercy in the soul.

4- It establishes equality between the rich and the poor, the noble and the common.

5- It trains the community in order, unity and harmony.

6- It eliminates deposited materials in the body, and thereby the health of the fasting person improves.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 185:

Explanation of the words:

Shahr Ramadan (the month of Ramadan): It is the ninth month of the lunar year. The word shahr (month) is derived from shuhra (fame, renown), and Ramadan is derived from ramadha al-sa'im, meaning when the fasting person's insides become scorched by thirst.

Alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an (in which the Qur'an was sent down): This is a statement of its virtue over other months, for the Qur'an was sent down in it, namely in the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) within it, according to the verse ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [al-Dukhan: 3] and the verse ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. It was sent down all at once from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) to the House of Honour (bayt al-'izza) in the lowest heaven, then it was sent down gradually, star by star (najman ba'da najm). The beginning of its revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was also in Ramadan.

Hudan lil-nas (a guidance for mankind): guiding people to that which perfects them and brings them happiness in both abodes.

Wa bayyinatin min al-huda wal-furqan (and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion): al-bayyinat is the plural of bayyina, and al-huda means guidance. The meaning is that the Qur'an was sent down as a guide for people, clarifying for them the path of guidance, making clear the way to success and salvation, and distinguishing for them between truth and falsehood in all matters of life.

Shahida al-shahr (whoever witnesses the month): the announcement of its sighting has come forth.

Fa-'iddatun min ayyam ukhar (then a number of other days): then he must make up the fast, equal to the number of days he broke it while ill or traveling.

Wa li-tukmilu al-'idda (and that you complete the period): making up the fast is required so that the count of the month is completed, thirty or twenty-nine days.

Wa li-tukabbiru Allah 'ala ma hadakum (and that you glorify Allah for having guided you): this takes place upon completing the fast of Ramadan, from the sighting of the crescent until returning from the 'Eid prayer. Takbir is prescribed and carries great reward. Its well-known form is: Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, wa lillahi al-hamd.

Wa la'allakum tashkurun (so that perhaps you will be grateful): He obligated the fast upon you and enjoined takbir upon you, so that by this you may be among those who are grateful to Allah the Exalted for His blessings, because gratitude is obedience.

The meaning of the noble verse:

When the Exalted mentioned in the previous verse that He had prescribed fasting upon the community of Islam, and that it is for a number of days, He clarified in this verse that the intended "numbered days" are the days of the blessed month of Ramadan, in which the Qur'an was sent down as a guide, clarifying the paths of guidance and distinguishing between truth and falsehood. So the Exalted said: ﴿The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion. So whoever among you witnesses the month﴾ — meaning the month of Ramadan. "Witnesses" means he was present and not traveling when the sighting of the Ramadan crescent was announced; he must fast it as an obligation, if he is responsible (mukallaf). Then He mentioned the excuses of illness and travel, and that whoever breaks his fast due to them must make up the same number of days. The Exalted informed that by permitting breaking the fast for the ill and the traveler He intends ease for the community and does not intend hardship for it; so to Him belongs all praise and all favour. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days. Allah intends for you ease, and does not intend for you hardship﴾.

Then the Exalted gave the reason for making up the fast by His saying "and that you complete the period," meaning the period of the days of Ramadan, this being the first reason; and secondly "and that you glorify Allah for having guided you," when you complete the fast with the sighting of the crescent of Shawwal; and finally "so that perhaps you will be grateful," the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾.

Lessons from the verse:

1- The virtue of the month of Ramadan and the virtue of the Qur'an.

2- The obligation of fasting Ramadan upon the responsible (mukallaf), who is the Muslim, sane, and adult, with the woman free from menstrual and postpartum bleeding.

3- The concession for the ill person who fears delay in recovery or an increase in illness, and for the traveler on a journey of the distance of shortening (qasr).

4- The obligation of making up the fast for one who broke it due to an excuse.

5- The ease of the Islamic Shari'a and its freedom from hardship and difficulty.

6- The legislation of takbir on the night and day of 'Eid, and this takbir is part of thanking for the blessing of being guided to Islam.

7- Acts of obedience are gratitude; whoever does not obey Allah and His Messenger is not grateful and is not counted among the grateful.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 186:

Explanation of the words:

Al-da'i (the one who calls): the one who asks his Lord for his need.

Fa-l-yastajibu li (so let them respond to Me): that is, let them answer My call when I summon them to obey Me and obey My Messenger, by doing what is commanded, abandoning what is forbidden, and drawing near to Me by performing acts of nearness and abandoning what brings about My displeasure.

Yarshudun (they may be rightly guided): by the perfection of the two faculties, the knowledge-based and the practical, for rushd (right guidance) is knowledge of what pleases Allah and what displeases Him, together with doing what pleases Him and abandoning what displeases Him. Whoever has neither knowledge nor action is the foolish, misguided one, the astray and the ruined.

The meaning of the noble verse:

It is narrated that a group of the Companions asked the Prophet, saying: "Is our Lord near, so that we may address Him in private supplication, or is He distant, so that we must call out to Him?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ to the end of the verse. Munajah (intimate conversation) means speaking with lowered voice, and munadah (calling out) means speaking with raised voice. Allah's responding to the invocation of His servant means accepting his request and granting what he seeks. What is incumbent upon the servants is only to respond to their Lord, by believing in Him and obeying Him in His commands and prohibitions, and by this their rightly guided path is completed, and they become qualified for perfection and felicity in both abodes, this world and the Hereafter.

Guidance from the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse:

1- The nearness of Allah the Exalted to His servants, for all worlds are in His grasp and under His authority, and nothing among His creation is far from Allah, for there is no existent except that Allah sees it, hears it, and has power over it; and this is the reality of nearness.

2- The disliking of raising the voice in acts of worship, except what is in the talbiyah (the call of the pilgrim), the adhan (call to prayer), and the iqamah (the second call to prayer).

3- The obligation to respond to Allah the Exalted with faith and righteous deeds.

4- Rushd (right guidance) lies in obeying Allah, while error (ghayy) and foolishness (safah) lie in disobeying Him the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 187:

Explanation of the words:

Laylat al-siyam (the night of fasting): the night after which the servant becomes one who is fasting.

Al-rafath: sexual intercourse.

Libas lakum (a garment for you): a metaphor for the intermingling of some of you with others, like the intermingling of a garment with the body.

Takhtanuna anfusakum (you were betraying yourselves): by exposing them to punishment and diminishing their share of reward, through intercourse on the night of fasting before God had made that permissible for you.

Bashiruhunna (have intercourse with them): He permitted them this at night.

Wabtaghu ma kataba Allah lakum (and seek what God has prescribed for you): seek through intercourse the child, if it has been decreed for you, and let intercourse not be merely for the sake of desire.

Al-khayt al-abyad (the white thread): the false dawn, which is a whiteness that appears on the horizon like the tail of a wolf (sirhan).

Al-khayt al-aswad (the black thread): a blackness that comes after the first whiteness and entirely abrogates it.

Al-fajr (the dawn): the spreading of light horizontally, which abrogates the blackness of the black thread and the brightness covers the whole horizon.

Akifun fi al-masajid (secluding themselves in the mosques): devoting themselves to worship in the mosque, seeking nearness to God, exalted is He.

Hudud Allah (the limits of God): plural of hadd, which is what God has legislated of acts of obedience, whether doing or abstaining.

Kadhalika yubayyinu Allah ayatihi (thus God makes His signs clear): that is, just as He clarified the rulings of fasting, He clarifies the rulings of all other acts of worship, both actions and abstentions, so that He prepares them for taqwa (God-consciousness), which is the cause that inherits Paradise.

Meaning of the noble verse:

At the beginning of the obligation of fasting, whoever slept at night did not eat, drink, or approach his wife until the following night. It was as if fasting began from sleep, not from the rising of dawn. Then some people went to their wives and informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of that. So God, exalted is He, revealed this noble verse permitting them to eat, drink, and have intercourse throughout the night until the rising of dawn. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives﴾, meaning the intermingling with them, since a man has no independence from his wife nor a woman from her husband. ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾: she covers him and he covers her, like a garment covering the body. He informed them that He knew what they had done of going in to their wives at night after sleeping, before the ruling of God concerning it had been revealed, either permitting or forbidding it, and that this was from them a betrayal of themselves. So He said: ﴿God knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾. Then He made the permission known to them by His saying: ﴿So now, have intercourse with them and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, meaning the child, because intercourse is not merely for the satisfaction of desire but for procreation and offspring. He specified for them the time in which they fast, which is the day from the rising of dawn until the setting of the sun, and He said: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn; then complete the fast until the night﴾. He forbade those secluding themselves in the mosques to have intercourse with their wives; it is not lawful for a man, while secluded, to leave the mosque and approach his wife, and if he does so he sins, his seclusion is invalidated, and he is obligated to make it up. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are secluding yourselves in the mosques﴾. He informed them that what He had made clear to them of obligations and prohibitions are the limits of God, so it is not lawful to draw near to them or to transgress them. He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿These are the limits of God, so do not approach them﴾. Then He said: ﴿Thus God makes clear His signs to the people that they may become God-fearing﴾. Thus God bestowed His favor upon the Muslims with this blessing, namely the clarification of the laws, rulings, and limits through what He revealed to His Messenger of the Book and the Sunnah, so as to prepare the believers for taqwa through that, since taqwa cannot exist unless there are laws to follow and limits to respect.

And He has done so; to Him be praise and to Him be grace.

Guidance from the verse:

1- Permissibility of eating, drinking, and intercourse during the nights of fasting, from sunset until the rising of dawn.

2- Clarification of the time of fasting, which is from the true dawn until sunset.

3- Clarification of what the fasting person refrains from: eating, drinking, and intercourse.

4- The legislation of i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), especially in Ramadan, and that the one in seclusion may not mix with his wife while in seclusion until the period of seclusion he resolved to observe has ended.

5- The use of metaphor instead of explicit wording regarding what is shameful to mention, where He used "mubashara" (intimate contact) as a metaphor for sexual intercourse.

6- The prohibition of violating the sanctity of the Sharia and transgressing its limits.

7- Clarification of the purpose of revealing the laws and establishing the limits, which is the God-consciousness of Almighty God.

8- Established by the Sunnah: the recommendation of suhur and of delaying it as long as one does not fear the dawn arriving, and the recommendation of hastening iftar.

**Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on Surah 2, Verse 188**

**Explanation of the words:**

*Al-batil* (falsehood): the opposite of *al-haqq* (truth).

*Tudlu* (you bring forward): *al-idla' bi-l-shay'* means casting or presenting a thing. Here it means giving bribes (*rishwah*, the payment given to gain an unjust ruling) to judges and rulers so that they will rule in their favour by falsehood, in order to reach the property of others.

*Fariqan* (a portion): that is, a group or a piece of wealth.

*Bi-l-ithm* (by sin): here it refers to bribery, false testimony (*shahadat al-zur*), and the perjurious oath (*al-yamin al-fajirah*), that is, swearing falsely so that the judge rules for you by falsehood in the appearance of truth.

**The meaning of the noble verse:**

When Allah, the Exalted, informed in the previous verse that He makes clear to people the rulings of His religion so that they may fear Him by performing what is commanded and abstaining from what is forbidden, He made clear in this verse the ruling on consuming the wealth of Muslims by falsehood. It is forbidden, and it is not lawful for a Muslim to take his brother's property without his genuine consent. He mentioned a type that is the worst form of consuming wealth by falsehood, which is paying bribes to judges and rulers so that they rule for them against the truth. Thus they involve the judges in ruling against the truth, and they consume the property of their brothers through false testimony and the *yamin al-ghamus*, the sinful perjurious oath, which is the one in which a person swears while lying.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth by falsehood, nor bring it forward to the rulers in order that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people sinfully while you know﴾, that is, while you know the prohibition of that.

**Guidance of the verse:**

From the guidance of the verse:

1. The prohibition of consuming the wealth of a Muslim without right, whether by theft, usurpation, cheating, or deception and sophistry.

2. The prohibition of bribery, which is paid to a ruler so that he rules against the truth.

3. The wealth of a non-combatant disbeliever is like the wealth of a Muslim in its sanctity, but the wealth of a Muslim is more sacred, because of the hadith: "All of a Muslim is forbidden to another Muslim: his blood, his honour, and his wealth," and because of Allah's words in this verse, ﴿and do not consume your wealth﴾, as He addresses the Muslims.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 189:

Explanation of the words:

Al-ahilla (ٱلأَهِلَّة): plural of hilal (crescent), which is the moon at the beginning of its appearance during the first three days of the month, because when people see it they raise their voices saying: "The crescent! The crescent!"

Al-mawaqit (ٱلْمَوَاقِيتُ): plural of miqat: the specified, known time for people.

Ityan al-buyut min zuhuriha (إتيان البيوت من ظهورها): that one climbs over the wall and enters the house, out of reluctance to enter through the door.

Wa-lakinna al-birra man ittaqa (ولكن البرّ من اتقى): the righteousness that leads to the pleasure of Allah is the righteousness of a servant who fears Allah, the Exalted, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So righteousness is not entering houses from their backs.

Al-falah (ٱلفلاح): success, which is salvation from the Fire and entry into Paradise.

The meaning of the noble verse:

It is narrated that some of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: "What is the matter with the crescent? It appears thin, then it grows until it becomes large and becomes a full moon, then it keeps diminishing until it returns as it was at its beginning?" So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿They ask you about the crescents.﴾ and commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them: they are times set for people and a sign, whose beginning is small, then it becomes complete, then it diminishes until the conjunction, so that people may know by them their appointed times for their affairs. By the presence of the moon in these states, the waiting periods of women are known, we know the months, so we know Ramadan and we know the month and time of Hajj, as we know the terms of contracts in sale and rent, the settlement of debts, and so on.

In the Jahiliyya, the Ansar, when one of them entered the state of ihram for Hajj or Umrah and left his house and wanted to enter for a specific purpose, he would not enter through the door, so that the lintel of the door would not shade him; he would climb over the wall and enter through the back of the house, not its door, and they considered this obedience and righteousness. So Allah, the Exalted, nullified this Jahili form of worship by His saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [that of] one who fears Allah.﴾ the righteousness of the people of piety and goodness. He commanded them to enter houses through their doors, saying: ﴿And enter houses through their doors﴾, and commanded them to be mindful of Him, the Exalted, so that they would prosper in this world and the Hereafter. He said: ﴿And fear Allah that you may succeed.﴾

Guidance from the noble verse:

From the guidance of the verse:

1- That a person should ask about what benefits him and leave aside questions about what does not concern him.

2- The benefit of the lunar months is great, for by them many acts of worship are known.

3- The prohibition of innovation in religion, even if it is done out of desire to obey Allah and obtain reward.

4- The command to piety, which leads to the servant's success and salvation in both abodes.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 190–193:

Explanation of the words:

Sabil Allah (the path of God): the way that leads to His pleasure, which is Islam; what is intended is raising high the word of God.

Alladhina yuqatilunakum (those who fight you): the polytheists who initiate fighting against you.

Wa la ta'tadu (and do not transgress): do not exceed the limit by killing women and children, or those who withdraw from fighting.

Thaqiftumuhum (you overcome them): you gain the ability to fight them.

Al-fitnah (sedition): polytheism (shirk).

Al-Masjid al-Haram (the Sacred Mosque): what is meant by it is Makkah and the Haram surrounding it.

Wa yakuna al-din lillah (and religion be for God): that no one remains who worships other than God the Exalted.

Fa la 'udwan (then there is no aggression): that is, there is no aggression through killing and warfare except against the wrongdoers. As for those who have embraced Islam, they are not to be fought.

Meaning of the verses:

These three verses: ﴿Fight in the way of God﴾ are among the first revealed concerning the fighting of the polytheists, and they include the permission given to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers to fight those who fight them and to refrain from those who refrain from fighting them. God the Exalted said: "Fight in the way of God," that is, in the way of raising high the word of God so that He alone is worshipped. "Those who fight you," and "kill them wherever you overcome them, and expel them from their homes as they expelled you, O emigrants, from your homes," and do not hesitate to kill, for their sedition against the believers, compelling them to disbelief through persecution and torture, is worse than killing. ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, so do not be the initiators; but if they fight you, then kill them. Likewise, the killing and expulsion inflicted by you upon them is the recompense of every disbeliever who transgresses and wrongs. Then if they desist from polytheism and disbelief and embrace Islam, God will forgive them and have mercy upon them, for God is Forgiving and Merciful.

As for the fourth verse [193], which is the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no sedition﴾, it confirms the ruling of the preceding verses, for in it is the command to fight the polytheists who fought them, a fighting that continues until no one remains in Makkah who is persecuted in his religion and tempted away from it, and the religion becomes entirely God's, so that none other than Him is worshipped. His saying "then if they desist" means: if they desist from polytheism by embracing Islam and affirming God's oneness, then refrain from them and do not fight them, for there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers, and after their conversion to Islam they have not become wrongdoers.

Guidance of the verses:

From the guidance of these verses:

1- The obligation to fight those who fight the Muslims, and to refrain from those who refrain from fighting them; this is before the abrogation of this verse.

2- The prohibition of transgression in fighting by killing children, the elderly and women, unless they fight.

3- The prohibition of fighting at the Sacred Mosque, that is Makkah and the Haram, unless the enemy initiates fighting there, in which case one fights.

4- Islam erases what came before it, based on God's saying: ﴿But if they desist, then God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

5- The obligation of jihad, which is a communal (kifaya) duty whenever there is a believer who is persecuted for his Islam or tempted away from his religion.

5- The obligation of jihad, which is a communal (kifaya) duty whenever there is a believer who is persecuted for his Islam or tempted away from his religion.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 194–195:

Explanation of the words:

Al-Shahr al-Haram (the sacred month): the month in which fighting is forbidden. The sacred months are four: three in succession and one standing alone. The three are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram, and the fourth, which stands alone, is Rajab.

Al-Hurumat (the sacred things): the plural of hurmah, as in al-shahr al-haram, al-balad al-haram (the sacred city) and al-ihram (the state of sanctity entered for pilgrimage).

Inna Allaha ma'a al-muttaqin (Indeed, Allah is with those who are mindful of Him): al-muttaqun (the God-fearing) are the believers who guard against disobedience to Allah the Exalted and against opposing His laws in life. His being with them, the Exalted, means that He guides them, aids them and grants them victory.

Al-Tahlukah (ruin): al-hulkah and al-halak have the same meaning.

Al-Ihsan (excellence): perfecting obedience and purifying it from the taints of association (shirk), and also doing good.

Meaning of the two verses:

The first verse [194], in the context of what precedes it, encourages the believers who have been attacked to fight their enemies. It teaches them that whoever fights them in the sacred month, they may fight him in the sacred month; whoever fights them in the sacred precinct, they may fight him in the sacred precinct; and whoever fights them while they are in a state of ihram, they may fight him while he is in a state of ihram. Likewise, the sacred things are subject to retaliation and equality among them. Whoever attacks them, they may attack him in the same measure as his attack upon them. He commanded them to be mindful of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and informed them that He is with them, so long as they are mindful of Him, by guiding, aiding and granting them victory.

As for the verse [195], He commanded them to spend wealth for jihad, to prepare equipment and to dispatch expeditionary forces and fighters. He forbade them to abandon spending in the way of Allah, which is jihad, for whenever they abandon spending and jihad, they become like one who casts his own hands into ruin. This is because the enemy lying in wait for them, when he sees them sitting back from jihad, will raid them, fight them and gain victory over them, and they will perish. He also commanded them to excel in all their deeds; excellence in deeds means perfecting and beautifying them and purifying them from defect and corruption. He promised them that if they excel in their deeds, He will support and grant them victory, saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do good; indeed, Allah loves those who do good﴾. Whoever Allah loves, He honours and grants victory, and He does not humiliate him nor forsake him.

Lessons of the two verses:

Among the lessons of the two verses:

1- Respect for the sacred month and all the sacred things.

2- The permissibility of retaliation and requital against one who has attacked, so that he is treated in the same way he treated others, measure for measure.

3- Repelling aggression and striking at the wrongdoer who initiates injustice and attack.

4- Allah's companionship with the people of faith, piety and excellence.

5- The virtue of excellence, because Allah loves those who do good.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 196:

Explanation of the words:

"And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah": Completing them means entering into ihram for them from the miqat (the designated boundary point), performing their pillars (arkan) and obligatory acts (wajibat) in the manner required by the Lawgiver (al-Shari'), and being sincere to Allah, the Exalted, in them.

"But if you are prevented": Hasr and ihsar mean that the pilgrim or the one performing 'Umrah is unable to complete his Hajj or 'Umrah, either because of an enemy who blocks him from entering Makkah, or because of a severe illness that prevents him from continuing the journey to Makkah.

"Then an offering that is easy to obtain": That is, what is obligatory upon the one who is prevented is whatever offering is available to him: a sheep, a cow, or a camel.

"And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice": The one who is prevented does not exit the state of ihram until he slaughters whatever offering is available to him. If he slaughters it, he exits the state of ihram by shaving his head.

"Then a ransom": The obligation is a ransom of fasting, almsgiving, or sacrifice (nusuk).

"Then whoever enjoys 'Umrah until Hajj": Whoever enters into ihram for 'Umrah during the months of Hajj, exits its state, remains in Makkah awaiting Hajj, and then actually performs Hajj, the obligation upon him is "what is easy to obtain of the offering."

"Then whoever cannot find one, [let him fast] three days": Whoever performs tamattu' (combining 'Umrah and Hajj) and cannot find an offering, due to his inability to obtain it, the obligation is to fast ten days: three in Makkah and seven in his own land.

"That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque": That is, what is obligatory of the offering or fasting in case of inability applies to those who are not people of the Haram. As for the residents of Makkah and the Haram around it, who are the people of the Haram, nothing is obligatory upon them if they perform tamattu'.

The meaning of the noble verse:

Allah, the Exalted, commands His believing servants to complete Hajj and 'Umrah for Him, the Glorified and Exalted, performing them in the required manner and intending by them Allah, the Exalted. He informs them that if they are prevented and are unable to complete them, then it is obligatory upon them to slaughter or sacrifice whatever is available to them; when they have slaughtered or sacrificed, they exit their state of ihram by shaving the hair of their heads or trimming it. He also informed them that whoever among them is ill or has an injury to his head and is forced to shave his head, or wear a garment, or cover his head, then after doing so the obligation is a ransom, which is one of three options at their choice: fasting three days, or feeding six needy persons, two handfuls of food for each needy person, or slaughtering a sheep. He also informed them that whoever performs tamattu' from 'Umrah to Hajj and is not a resident of the Haram, upon him is what is easy to obtain of the offering: a sheep, a cow, or a camel; if he cannot find that, he fasts three days during Hajj, from the first of the month of Hajj until the ninth day of it, and seven days when he returns to his homeland. He commanded them to fear Him, the Mighty and Majestic, which means obeying His commands and adhering to His legislation, and warned them against neglecting His command and treating His law lightly, so He said: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾.

Guidance from the verse:

Among the guidance of the verse:

1- The obligation to complete Hajj and 'Umrah for whoever has begun them by entering ihram from the miqat, even if Hajj is voluntary and 'Umrah is not obligatory.

2- Explanation of the ruling on ihsar, which is slaughtering a sheep at the place of ihsar, then exiting ihram by shaving or trimming, then making up the performance in a later year if this is feasible for the servant, because the Messenger ﷺ and his companions made up the 'Umrah from which they were prevented from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah.

3- Explanation of the ransom for harm (fidyat al-adha), which is that whoever commits one of the prohibited acts of ihram, such as shaving, wearing stitched clothing, or covering his head due to an excuse, is obligated to a ransom, which is fasting, feeding, or slaughtering a sheep.

4- Detailed explanation of the ruling on tamattu', which is that whoever is not a resident of Makkah or the Haram around it, if he enters into ihram for 'Umrah during the months of Hajj, exits from it, remains in Makkah, and performs Hajj in the same year, is obligated to slaughter a sheep; if he is unable, he fasts three days in Makkah and seven in his homeland.

5- The command to taqwa, which is obedience to Allah, the Exalted, by carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibition, and a warning against abandoning it because of the severe punishment that follows from it.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 197–199:

Explanation of the words:

Ashhur ma'lumat (well-known months): they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. These are the months in which one enters the state of ihram for Hajj.

Fard (obligation): one intends Hajj and enters the state of ihram for it.

Fala rafath (then no obscenity): rafath is sexual intercourse and its preliminaries.

Wa la fusuq (nor wickedness): fisq and fusuq mean going out of obedience to Allah by abandoning an obligation or committing a prohibited act.

Al-jidal (disputing): quarrelling and contention.

Al-junah (sin): wrongdoing.

Tabtaghu fadlan (you seek bounty): you seek profit through trade during Hajj.

Afadtum min Arafat (you pour forth from Arafat): the departure from Arafat takes place after standing at Arafat on the day of Hajj, that is, after sunset on the ninth day of Dhu al-Hijjah.

Al-Mash'ar al-Haram (the sacred landmark): Muzdalifah. Remembrance of Allah there means the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers combined there, and the Fajr prayer.

Meaning of the verses:

The context still concerns the rulings of Hajj and 'Umrah. Allah, exalted is He, informs that Hajj has well-known months, namely Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah, so one enters the state of ihram for Hajj only within them. Whoever enters ihram for Hajj must avoid obscenity, wickedness, and disputing, so that his Hajj is not spoiled or his reward diminished. He also urges the pilgrim to do good, such as charity and other deeds, saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾, and it follows that He will reward him for it and recompense him. He commands the pilgrims to take provision for their journey in Hajj, of food and drink by which they keep their faces free from asking, saying: "And take provision," and he guides them to the best provision, which is taqwa (God-consciousness). Among taqwa is not asking people for their wealth, while the servant is not in need. He commands them to fear Him, exalted and mighty, that is, to be mindful of Him so that they do not disobey Him in His commands and prohibitions, saying: ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾. Allah is most worthy of being feared, for He is the One, the Subduer. Then He permitted them to trade while they are in Makkah and Mina, saying: ﴿There is no sin upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord﴾, meaning lawful provision through permissible trade. Then He commanded them to remember Allah at Muzdalifah with the Maghrib, 'Isha' and Fajr prayers there, after their pouring forth from Arafat following sunset, saying, Mighty is He who speaks: ﴿So when you pour forth from Arafat, remember Allah at the sacred landmark﴾. Then He reminded them of the blessing of His guidance to them after the misguidance they were in, and urged them to thank Him by remembering Him much, saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you, though before it you were among the astray﴾. Then He commanded them to equality in standing at Arafat and departing from it, so that all of them stand at Arafat and all of them depart from it together, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then pour forth from where the people pour forth﴾. This was because the Hums used to depart from the nearest part of Arafat so that they would escape the crowding and be safe from the crush. Finally, He commanded them to seek forgiveness from Allah, that is, to ask Him for forgiveness, and promised them forgiveness by saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

Guidance from the verses:

1- The sanctity of obscenity, wickedness, and disputing during ihram.

2- The recommendation for the pilgrim to do good deeds during his Hajj, so that his reward is magnified and his Hajj is accepted.

3- The permissibility of trade and work for the pilgrim seeking provision, provided he does not perform Hajj for that purpose.

4- The obligation of spending the night at Muzdalifah for the remembrance of Allah.

5- The obligation of thanking Allah by remembering Him and obeying Him for His guidance and favour.

6- The obligation of equality in performing the rites of Hajj among all pilgrims, so that none of them is distinguished from another in any rite of Hajj.

7- Encouragement to seek forgiveness and to do so often.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 200–203:

Explanation of the words:

Qadaytum (قضيتم): You performed them and finished them.

Al-manasik (المناسك): Plural of mansak (منسك), which refers to the various acts of worship of the Hajj.

Al-khalaq (الخلاق): Share and portion.

Hasanah (حسنة): The good of this world is everything that pleases and does no harm, such as a righteous wife, a righteous child, and lawful provision. The good of the Hereafter is salvation from the Fire and entry into the Gardens.

Qina (قنا): Protect us and save us from the punishment of the Fire.

Nasib (نصيب): A share and portion of their righteous deeds and their righteous supplication.

Al-ayyam al-ma'dudat (الأيام المعدودات): The three days of tashriq (أيام التشريق) after the day of Eid.

Ta'ajjala fi yawmayn (تعجل في يومين): He threw the pebbles on the first and second days and travelled.

Wa man ta'akhkhara (ومن تأخر): He threw the pebbles on all three days.

Fa la ithm (فلا إثم): That is, there is no sin in hastening or in delaying.

Li-man ittaqa (لمن اتقى): For the one who fears his Lord by not abandoning an obligation He has imposed or committing a prohibition He has forbidden.

Tuhsharun (تحشرون): You will be gathered for reckoning and recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

The meaning of the verses:

With these four verses, the discussion of the rulings of Hajj comes to an end. In the first verse [200], the Exalted instructs the believers, when they have finished their rites, by throwing the pebble at Jamrat al-Aqabah, sacrificing, performing the Tawaf al-Ifadah, and settling in Mina for rest and relaxation, that they should remember God abundantly at the throwing of the pebbles and upon leaving the prayers, with a remembrance that is greatly abundant, in the manner that they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when they would recount the glories of their fathers and the nobility of their forefathers. The Exalted then explains their condition: among them is one whose concern is only the world, so he asks God only for what concerns him of it, and this was the state of most pilgrims in the Jahiliyyah; and among them is one who asks God for the good of this world and the Hereafter, and they are the believing monotheists, who say: ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. This includes teaching and guiding the believers to this comprehensive supplication and this beneficial, righteous aim, so to God belongs all praise and grace. In the verse [202], the Exalted informs that for the people of righteous supplication, who are the believing monotheists, there is a share of reward for their deeds that they earned in this world, and He is swift in reckoning, so He hastens for them the advance of reward, which is Paradise. In the verse [203], the Exalted commands His servants, the believing pilgrims, to remember Him on the days of tashriq, at the throwing of the pebbles and after the five prayers, saying: "God is greatest, God is greatest, there is no god but God; God is greatest, God is greatest, and to God belongs praise," three times, until the afternoon of the third day of tashriq. Then God informed them that there is no blame upon one who hastens his departure to his family after throwing on the second day, just as there is no blame upon one who delays and throws on the third day. So He said: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾. The matter is thus one of choice, and the negation of sin is conditioned by piety toward Him, the Mighty and Majestic: whoever abandons an obligation or commits a prohibited act, upon him is the sin of his disobedience, and nothing purifies him from it except repentance. So the negation of sin is restricted only to hastening or not hastening. His saying, "for the one who is pious," is therefore a beautiful condition, and so they should prepare for that by remembering Him, thanking Him, and eagerly seeking to obey Him.

Guidance of the verses:

Among the guidance of the verses:

1- The obligation of remembrance in Mina at the throwing of the pebbles, as one proclaims "God is greatest" with each pebble.

2- The virtue of remembrance and desire for it, because it is among the things beloved to God.

3- The virtue of asking God for both goods and not limiting oneself to one of them, and the blameworthiness of limiting oneself to seeking the world and its debris.

4- The virtue of the supplication ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. It comprises both goods together, and the Prophet ﷺ would conclude with it every circuit when he circumambulated the House.

5- The obligation of spending three nights in Mina and the obligation of throwing the pebbles, since through them remembrance of God on the counted days, which are the days of tashriq, is achieved.

6- The concession to hasten for one who throws on the second day.

7- The command to fear God and the remembrance of the gathering, reckoning, and recompense, since this remembrance helps one attain the piety of the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 200–203:

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 204–207:

Explanation of the words:

Yu'jibuka (يعجبك): it pleases you and you find it fine.

Fi al-dunya (في الدنيا): when he speaks about the affairs of this worldly life.

Alad al-khisam (ألد الخصام): fierce in contention, strong in dispute, owing to the glibness of his tongue.

Tawalla (تولى): he turned back and departed, or he held authority.

Al-harth wa al-nasl (الحرث والنسل): al-harth means crops, and al-nasl means animals.

Akhathat-hu al-'izzah bi al-ithm (أخذته العزة بالإثم): zeal and arrogance seized him on account of his sins, so he does not fear Allah.

Yashri nafsahu (يشري نفسه): he sells his self to Allah, the Exalted, by striving in His cause with his self and his wealth.

Meaning of the verses:

Allah, the Exalted, informs His Messenger and the believers about the condition of the hypocrites and of the sincere believers. He says, addressing the Messenger ﷺ: "And among the people is a man, a hypocrite, who makes his speech pleasing, and when he speaks, you are pleased with his words, because of the polish and splendour that they have. This is when he speaks about the affairs of the life of this world, unlike the affairs of the Hereafter, for he is ignorant of them and has no impetus to speak about them, since he is a disbeliever. And when he speaks, he calls Allah to witness that he believes what he says, and says to the Messenger ﷺ, 'Allah knows that I am a believer and that I love you,' and calls Allah to witness, 'that I am such-and-such...' And when he leaves your gathering and departs from you, ﴿he strives in the land﴾, that is, he walks in it with corruption, to destroy the crops and the animals by committing grave crimes, so that rain is withheld, the harvests wither, the land becomes barren, the beasts die, and offspring are cut off. And this deed of his is hated by Allah, the Exalted, so He does not love it nor the one who does it." Allah, the Exalted, also informs that when this hypocrite is commanded to do good or forbidden from evil, and it is said to him, "Fear Allah, do not do such-and-such, or leave such-and-such," he is seized by arrogance and zeal on account of the sins with which he is afflicted, so he does not fear Allah and does not turn to Him in repentance. Hell is sufficient recompense for his hypocrisy, his evil and his corruption; he spreads it as a bed from which he never departs, forever. ﴿And how wretched is the resting-place, Hell.﴾

Allah, the Exalted, also informs about the sincere believer, saying: "And among the people is a man, a believer of true faith, who sold his self and his wealth to Allah, seeking His pleasure and life in His neighbourhood in the Garden, the Abode of Peace." So Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is Kind to His servants.﴾ That is, Merciful to them.

It is said that the hypocrite man whose description is contained in the first three verses is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and that the believing man whose description is contained in the fourth verse [207] is Suhayb ibn Sinan al-Rumi, Abu Yahya. When the polytheists learned that he intended to emigrate to Madinah to join the Messenger ﷺ and his Companions, they said, "You will not go off with your self and your wealth to Muhammad. We will not allow you to emigrate unless you give us all your wealth." So he gave them all that he possessed and emigrated. When he reached Madinah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw him, he said to him: "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya; the sale has profited." Although the verses were revealed concerning al-Akhnas and Suhayb, the lesson lies in the generality of the wording and not in the specificity of the occasion. Al-Akhnas is an example of evil for everyone who has his characteristics, and Suhayb is an example of goodness and perfection for everyone who has his characteristics.

Guidance of the verses:

From the guidance of the verses:

1- A warning against being deceived by the eloquence and articulateness of a man who is not among the people of faith and sincerity.

2- The worst of people is he who corrupts the land by committing crimes, which causes corruption and destruction to people and livestock.

3- A man's saying "Allah knows" or "Allah bears witness" counts as an oath, so the believer should beware of saying it while knowing himself to be lying.

4- When a believer is told "Fear Allah," it is obligatory for him not to be angry or to resent the one who commands him to piety; rather he must acknowledge his sin, seek Allah's forgiveness, and immediately give up the disobedience.

5- Encouragement to strive in the cause of Allah with one's self and wealth, and the permissibility for a Muslim to give up all his wealth in the cause of Allah, without this being considered extravagance or wastefulness, since extravagance and wastefulness are in spending on sins and wrongdoing.
