Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 258:

Explanation of the words:

"Alam tara" (Have you not considered): Has it not reached your knowledge, O our Messenger? The interrogative form expresses wonder at the tyrant who argued with Ibrahim.

Hajja (argued): debated, disputed, and contended.

Fi rabbihi (concerning his Lord): concerning the matter of his Lord, regarding His existence, His lordship, and His divinity over all creation.

Atahu Allah al-mulk (Allah had given him the kingdom): He had given him rule and sovereignty over the people of his land and the dwellings of his nation.

Ibrahim: He is the father of the prophets, Ibrahim al-Khalil (the Friend of Allah), peace be upon him. This argument took place before Ibrahim's migration to the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria).

Fa-bahita alladhi kafara (so the one who disbelieved was confounded): That disbelieving tyrant was silenced from the argument, bewildered and dumbfounded. He was Namrud al-Babili (Nimrod of Babylon).

Meaning of the noble verse:

When Allah the Exalted mentioned His guardianship over His allies, that He supports and aids them and brings them out of darkness into light, He gave an example of this: the argument of Namrud against Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Allah the Exalted said, addressing His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): "Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim concerning his Lord?" That is, has the argument of that tyrant not reached your knowledge, the one whom the blessing of kingship, which We gave him as a test, made arrogant, so he disbelieved, claimed lordship, and argued with Our Friend. Indeed, it is a strange matter. When Ibrahim said to him, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Ibrahim answered his argument, saying, "My Lord brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." Thus he was confounded, bewildered, and silenced, and Allah supported His friend Ibrahim and he prevailed. This is an example of Allah bringing His allies out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge.

Guidance from the verse:

1. Blessings make their possessor arrogant when he is deprived of the guardianship of Allah the Exalted.
2. Allah supports His allies and inspires them with proof to defeat their enemies.
3. When a servant wrongs and adheres to wrongdoing until it becomes his attribute, he is deprived of Allah's guidance and never finds guidance.
4. Permissibility of debate and disputation in establishing sound and correct belief.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 259:

Explanation of the words:

Qarya (a town): a city whose name Allah the Exalted did not mention, so one should not search for it, since knowing it brings no benefit.

Khawiya (in ruins): empty of its inhabitants, its roofs fallen onto its buildings and walls.

Anna yuhyi (how will He give life): how will He revive it.

Ba'da mawtiha (after its death): after its desolation and its roofs falling in.

Labitha (he remained): he stayed and lingered.

Lam yatasanna (it had not changed): it had not been altered by the passing of the years.

Aya (a sign): a proof of Allah's power to raise people alive on the Day of Resurrection.

Nunshizuha: in the recitation of Warsh, it is read as nunshiruha, meaning we revive it after its death. Nunshizuha means we raise it up and gather it together so that it becomes a donkey as it was.

Meaning of the verse:

This is another example, coordinated with the first one, in which the reality of Allah's guardianship (wilaya) toward Ibrahim was made manifest, when He supported him with a decisive proof and gave him victory over his enemy Nimrod. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town while it was in ruins﴾, empty of its inhabitants, its roofs fallen onto its buildings. So the passer-by said, deeming its revival a remote possibility a second time: "How will Allah bring this town back to life after its ruin?" So Allah caused him to die for one hundred years, then revived him, and asked him: "How long have you remained?" He said: according to the habit of one who sleeps during the day and wakes up in it, he thinks he slept a day or part of a day.

He answered him, correcting his understanding: "Rather, you have remained one hundred years. And so that you may be convinced of what you were told, look at your food, a basket of figs, and your drink, grape juice, for its taste and color have not changed, though a century has passed over it. And look at your donkey, for it has perished with the passage of time and nothing of it remains but its bones, glistening white. This is a decisive proof of its death and annihilation after one hundred years had passed over it. And look at the bones, how We assemble them and clothe them with flesh, and behold, they become your donkey that you rode one hundred years ago, when you slept and left it beside you grazing." Thus the power of Allah the Exalted was manifested in the non-change of what customarily changes within a single day, namely the basket of figs and the grape juice, and in the change of what customarily changes only over decades of years, namely the donkey. This is also evident in the death of its owner and his revival after lying dead on the face of the earth for one hundred years, without anyone finding him. After having shown him the manifestations of His power, the Lord, blessed and exalted, said to him: "We did this to you so that We may show you Our power to revive the town whenever We wish to revive it, and so that We may make you a sign to the people in your story, guiding them to faith in Us, to the unity of Our worship, and to Our power to resurrect in the Last Life, which there is no doubt about, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned."

Finally, when the lights of Allah's guardianship shone in the heart of this believing servant, whose wonder at the ruin of the town had led him to deem its revival remote, he said: "I know that Allah is over all things capable." This is the fulfilment of His saying: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ [al-Baqara: 257].

Guidance of the verse

From the guidance of the verse:

1- It is permissible for a servant to find something remote, even while he believes that it is true and will certainly occur, just as this believer who passed by the town found the revival of the town remote after witnessing its ruin and desolation.

2- The great power of Allah the Exalted, such that nothing can outmatch Him, for He is over all things capable.

3- The establishment and affirmation of the Last Life (resurrection).

4- The guardianship of Allah the Exalted toward the righteous believing servant was manifested in removing the darkness that appeared on the believer's heart through his deeming remote Allah's power to revive the town; so Allah showed him some manifestations of His power, which he declared in His saying: ﴿I know that Allah is over all things capable﴾.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 260:

Explanation of the words:

Ibrahim: he is Khalil al-Rahman (the Friend of the Most Merciful), father of the prophets, peace be upon him.

Yatma'inna qalbi (so that my heart may be at rest): it settles and calms down from longing and yearning to know the how.

Fa-surhunna ilayka (then take them to yourself): gather them and hold them close to you, and cut them into pieces.

Sa'yan (swiftly): running swiftly, or flying.

Aziz (Mighty): overpowering, from whom nothing can be withheld or escape, and nothing He wills is ever prevented in any circumstance.

Hakim (Wise): He does not create in vain, nor does anything come into being without His wisdom, and He does not place anything other than in its fitting place.

Meaning of the noble verse:

This is a third parable addressed to the Messenger and the believers, in which His guardianship over His believing servants is made manifest, bringing them out of darkness into light, even if the darkness is merely the thinking that something is beyond the power of God, or the yearning to know the manner in which something is brought into being and its form. So God the Exalted says: Remember ﴿when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ Abraham asked his Lord to show him the method of giving life: how it is accomplished, whether it follows fixed laws or is simply a power by which its Possessor says to a thing, "Be," and it is. His Lord, who knows him fully, asked him: do you not believe what you say? Abraham said: "Yes, I believe that You are Powerful over all things, but I want to see a manifestation of that by which my heart may be at rest and my longing and yearning to know what is unknown to me may be stilled." So God, as a response to him, since he was His friend, did not wish to leave him yearning about how his Lord gives life to the dead. He commanded him to take four birds, slaughter them, cut them into pieces, mix them together, and then place a quarter of the mixed pieces on each of four mountains. He did so. Then he took the head of each bird separately and called to it, and its scattered parts, mixed with the parts of the others, gathered together and came to him running, and he presented its head to it, and it joined to it and flew into the sky, while Abraham watched and witnessed the signs of the power of his Lord, the Mighty, the Wise. Glory be to Him; there is no god but Him and no lord besides Him.

Guidance of the noble verse:

From the guidance of the noble verse:

1- The human instinct to love knowing the unknown and to yearn for it.

2- God's guardianship of Abraham, in that He showed him of His signs what set his heart at rest and calmed his soul.

3- Confirmation of the doctrine of the second life, by the resurrection of creatures alive for reckoning and recompense.

4- Increase of faith and certainty whenever the servant contemplates God's cosmic signs, or recites and reflects upon God's Qur'anic verses.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 261–263:

Explanation of the words:

"The likeness of those who spend" (مثل الذين ينفقون): their praiseworthy and wondrous description.

"In the way of Allah" (سبيل الله): everything that leads to the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, from faith and righteous deeds.

"Multiplies" (يضاعف): increases and grows, until a thing becomes many times what it was.

"Reminder [of benefit] and harm" (منّاً ولا أذى): al-mann is mentioning the charity and enumerating it to the one to whom it was given, in a manner of showing superiority over him. Al-adha is belittling the recipient of charity and humiliating him with a harsh word or one that touches his dignity and lowers his honor.

"Kind speech" (قول معروف): good words said to a needy beggar, such as: "May Allah provide for us and for you," "Allah is Generous," "May Allah open [His bounties] for us and for you."

"And forgiveness" (ومغفرة): concealing the poor person's poverty by not making it apparent, and pardoning his bad manners if he has them.

"Rich" (غني): a self-sufficient richness, such that one never needs anything.

"Forbearing" (حليم): He does not hasten to punish; rather He pardons and overlooks.

Meaning of the verses:

Allah, the Exalted, informs us, encouraging striving with wealth, since it precedes striving with the self, because equipment comes first and men second, that the likeness of what the believer spends in the way of Allah, which here is jihad, in its growth, blessing and multiplication, is like a grain of wheat sown in good soil, which produces seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, so that one grain yields seven hundred grains. Likewise, a single dirham that the believer spends in the way of Allah is multiplied up to seven hundredfold, and it may be multiplied further, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾.

This is what the first verse [261] contains. As for the second verse [262], it carries the good news from Allah, the Exalted, for those who spend in His way and do not follow what they have spent with reminders of benefit or harm toward those to whom they gave, that there will be no fear upon them regarding what they will face in their lives, nor will they grieve over what they leave behind and what they forfeit. This is happiness, since their lives are free of fear and grief, and security and joy take their place. Finally, the third verse [263], which is ﴿a kind word and forgiveness...﴾: Allah, the Exalted, informs us that a good word said to the poor person, which opens his chest and gladdens his soul, is better than wealth given as charity to him by which he is humiliated and abased, so that he feels the bitterness of poverty more and the pain of need more severely. Forgiveness and concealment of his condition, avoiding his disgrace, or pardoning his bad manners, such as his insistence in asking, is also better than a charity by which he is exposed, reproached and denounced. His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿And Allah is Rich, Forbearing﴾ means: He is independent of creation, and Forbearing, He does not hasten to punish those who oppose His command.

Guidance from the verses:

1- The virtue of spending in jihad, and that it is the best of expenditures.

2- The virtue of charity and its praiseworthy consequences.

3- The prohibition of reminding of benefit after giving charity. In the hadith: "Three will not enter Paradise..." and he mentioned among them the one who reminds of his benevolence (al-mannan).

4- The gracious response to the poor person when nothing is available to give him, and likewise pardoning his harsh speech, from him or from others, is better than a charity followed by harm. In the hadith: "A good word is charity."

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 264:

Explanation of the words:

Ibtal al-sadaqah (nullifying charity): depriving oneself of its reward.

Al-mann wa al-adha (reminding of favours and harm): their meanings have already been mentioned.

Ri'a' al-nas (showing off to people): making a display before them in order to gain their praise or to ward off their blame.

Safwan (smooth rock): a smooth stone.

Wabil (heavy rain): intense rain.

Saldan (bare): smooth, with no dust upon it at all.

La yaqdiruna (they are unable): they are incapable of benefiting from anything of their false charities.

Meaning of the verse:

After He had encouraged charity and warned against what nullifies its reward, namely reminding of favours and causing harm, Exalted is He called out to His believing servants, saying: ﴿O you who have believed...﴾, forbidding them from corrupting their charities and nullifying their reward, so He said: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders or injury﴾, likening the nullification of charities to the case of the charity of the one who shows off, who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day, in their being nullified, so He said: ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. He also struck an example for the nullification of the charity of those who follow their charity with reminders or harm, or who show off with it before people, or who are disbelievers who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day, so He said: ﴿So his example is like a smooth rock with dust upon it﴾, meaning a smooth stone with dust on it, ﴿and heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare﴾, meaning intense rain fell upon it and removed the dust from it, leaving it smooth, bare, with nothing on it. Likewise, false charities are wiped away, and nothing remains of them for their owner to benefit from on the Day of Resurrection. So Exalted is He said: ﴿They are unable to obtain anything of what they have earned﴾, meaning of what they gave in charity, ﴿and Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, to what would make them happy and perfect, because of their disbelief in Him, Exalted is He.

Guidance of the verse

From the guidance of the verse:

1- The prohibition of reminders of favours and harm in charity, and that they corrupt it.

2- The nullification of the charity of one who reminds of favours, and of one who causes harm, and of one who shows off with it.

3- The prohibition of showing off, which is a form of shirk, according to the hadith: "Beware of showing off, for it is the minor shirk."

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 265–266:

Explanation of the words:

Al-mathal (the parable): a description that is pleasing and striking.

Ibtigha' mardat Allah (seeking the pleasure of God): seeking the approval of God, Exalted.

Tathbitan (strengthening/assurance): certainty and firm conviction in God's reward for them for their spending in His cause.

Jannatun bi-rabwah (a garden on a height): an orchard with many trees in an elevated place.

Di'fayn (twofold): doubled twice, or twice what other gardens yield.

Al-wabil (heavy rain): abundant, intense rain.

Al-tall (light rain): gentle rain.

I'sar (whirlwind): a violent wind containing scorching heat.

Meaning of the two verses:

When God mentioned the failure of those who spend their wealth to be seen by people, warning the believers against this, He, exalted be He, encouraged spending whereby the servant seeks God's pleasure and the otherworldly reward with Him. So He said, presenting this as a parable: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God﴾, i.e., seeking His pleasure, ﴿and assurance from themselves﴾, i.e., certainty and firm conviction on their part that God will reward them for it, ﴿is like a garden on an elevated place. Heavy rain strikes it, and it yields its produce twofold﴾, i.e., more than other gardens yield. Since this garden is in an elevated, high place, if heavy rain does not reach it, then dew and gentle, light rain suffice for its watering and irrigation, until it brings forth its fruit doubled twice. God concluded this noble statement with His saying: ﴿And God is Seeing of what you do﴾. Thus He promised those who spend seeking His pleasure and assurance from themselves great reward and good recompense, and He threatened those who spend and follow their spending with reproach and harm, and those who spend to be seen by people with loss and ruin.

This was the meaning of the first verse [265]. As for the second verse [266], God questions His servants in order to train them, refine their character, and elevate them to the stages of spiritual perfection. He says: ﴿Would one of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, beneath which rivers flow, and in which he has all kinds of fruits, while he has reached old age and become a very old man?﴾, i.e., would any of you, O spenders who spend not for the pleasure of God, love to have such a garden, while he has advanced in years and become an elderly man? Despite this weakness, he has small offspring who cannot earn and secure their own livelihood. Then that garden, which is the source of livelihood for the father and his children, is struck by a violent wind carrying the heat of scorching blasts, which reaches that garden and burns it. How would the state of the old man and his young children be? So too is the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people: he loses it all at a time when he is more in need of it than the old man and his small children, and that is the Day of Resurrection. Finally, God bestows favor upon His servants by clarifying for them the signs concerning beliefs, acts of worship, dealings, and manners, so that they may reflect upon them and be guided by their light to their perfection and happiness. So He said: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect﴾, i.e., thus is the clarification.

Guidance from the two verses:

1- The commendability of coining parables to bring meanings closer to minds so that they may benefit from them.

2- The doubling of the reward of charity free from reproach, harm, and showing off before people.

3- The invalidity of the charity of the one who reproaches, the one who harms, and the one who shows off, and the absence of any benefit from it.

4- The obligation to reflect upon the signs of God, especially those that carry the clarification of beliefs, rulings, manners, and morals.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 267–269:

Explanation of the words:

"From the good things you have earned": from the best and most excellent of your wealth.

"And from what We have brought forth for you from the earth": from grains and various kinds of fruit.

"And do not aim at the bad": do not intend the inferior, spending from it.

"Unless you would close your eyes to it": unless you overlook its inferiority and accept it with leniency and tolerance on your part.

"Ḥamīd" (Praiseworthy): praised in the earth and the heavens, in this world and the next, for the blessings He has bestowed and continues to bestow upon His creation.

"Satan threatens you with poverty": he frightens you with poverty, to prevent you from spending in the way of God.

"And orders you to immorality": he calls you to commit abominations, and among them is stinginess and avarice.

"Ḥikmah" (wisdom): understanding the secrets of the Sharia, and memorising the Book and the Sunnah.

"Ulu al-Albab" (people of understanding): people of sound, reflective minds who think about what benefits them.

The meaning of the verses:

After God had encouraged His believing servants to spend in His way in the previous verse, He addresses them here by the title of faith and commands them to give out the zakat of their wealth from the best of what they earn, saying: ﴿O you who believe, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾. He means grains and fruits; what they earn includes gold and silver and livestock, camels, cattle and sheep. He forbade them to give in charity from their inferior wealth, saying: ﴿And do not aim at the bad to spend from it, while you would not take it yourselves unless you close your eyes to it﴾. He means: it is not proper for you to spend the inferior, for if you were given it as a right of your own you would not accept it, were it not that you overlook it and accept it with leniency. This is from Him, a discipline and training for them. Finally, He informed them that He is free of need of His creation and their expenditures; He did not command them to pay zakat and give charity because He needs it, but He commanded them for their own completion and happiness, and that He is Ḥamīd, praised for the blessings He bestows upon all His creation. This is the meaning of verse [267].

As for verse [268], God warns His servants against Satan and his whisperings. He informed them that Satan threatens them with poverty, that is, frightens them of it, so that they do not pay zakat or give charity, and orders them to immorality, so that they spend their wealth in evil and corruption and withhold it from good and the public benefit. As for Him, by commanding them to spend, He promises them the forgiveness of their sins, for charity expiates sin, and bounty from Him, which is abundant and good provision. And He is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing of His creation. So respond, O believers, to the call of God, and turn away from the call of Satan, for he is your enemy and promises you only evil, and commands you only to wrongdoing and falsehood. This is what the second verse contains.

As for the third verse (269), God encourages the learning of beneficial knowledge, the knowledge that leads to righteous action, and this is none other than the knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah, by memorising them, understanding them and gaining jurisprudence in them. So He says: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾, that is, He, may He be exalted, gives wisdom to whomever He wills of those who seek it, who turn to it eagerly, asking God to teach them. He informs us finally that whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good, so the intelligent person should seek wisdom before seeking the world. This is a reminder: ﴿but none will be reminded except those of understanding﴾.

Guidance from the verses:

1- The obligation of zakat on silver and gold and what stands in their place from trade goods, and on livestock of camels, cattle and sheep, since all of these fall under His words ﴿what you have earned﴾, on condition of the lunar year passing and reaching the threshold (nisab).

2- The obligation of zakat on crops: grains and fruits, when they reach the threshold; likewise on minerals, since the phrase "what is brought forth from the earth" includes them.

3- The ugliness of giving from the inferior while leaving the good.

4- Warning against Satan, and the obligation to struggle against him by turning away from his whisperings and opposing his commands.

5- Responding to the call of God and acting by His guidance.

6- The superiority of knowledge over wealth.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 270–271:

Explanation of the words:

"Min nafaqah" (whatever expenditure): he means little or much, of good or of bad quality.

"Min nadhr" (whatever vow): the nadhr (vow) is a believer's binding of himself to something the Lawgiver did not make obligatory upon him, such as saying: "For Allah, it is incumbent upon me to give charity of a thousand, or to fast a month, or to pray such-and-such number of rak'ahs," or saying: "If such-and-such good comes to me, I will perform such-and-such acts of obedience."

"In tubdu al-sadaqat" (if you display the charities): i.e., if you make them apparent.

"Fa-ni'ma hiya" (then excellent is it): then excellent is that charity which you display, so that you may be emulated in it.

"Wa yukaffiru 'ankum min sayyi'atikum" (and He will remit from you some of your misdeeds): "yukaffiru" means He covers them and does not hold them to account for them; and "min" is partitive, since the rights of people are not expiated by charity.

Meaning of the noble verses:

After calling His servants to spend in the previous verse, the Exalted informed that He knows what His servants spend. If what is spent is good and righteous, He knows it and rewards for it; and if it is bad and inferior, He knows it and rewards for it. The Exalted said, addressing His believing servants: ﴿And whatever you spend of expenditure or vow of any vow, indeed Allah knows it﴾. So what was sought thereby the Face of Allah and was of good wealth, then it will expiate misdeeds and raise degrees; and what was inferior, or a vow made to other than the Exalted, then its people are wrongdoers, and they will be made to bear the wages of their expenditures and vows made to other than Allah, and they will not find anyone to reward them for any of it, because they are wrongdoers in it, in that they placed them in other than their proper place. ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. This is what the first verse [270] contained.

As for the second verse [271], the Exalted informed His believing servants that what they spend seeking His Face and from the good of their wealth, openly and publicly, is profitable wealth and an accepted expenditure for which its giver is rewarded. However, whatever of those expenditures is done secretly and placed in the hands of the poor is better for its giver, because it is far from the taint of ostentation, and because of honoring the poor and not exposing them to the humiliation of being given charity. And He, the Exalted, expiates for the spenders their misdeeds through their charities. He informed that He is Knowing of their deeds, and this was a reassurance to them of obtaining the rewards of their charities and all their other righteous deeds.

Guidance from the two verses:

1. Encouragement to give charity even if it is little, and a warning against ostentation in it, and against giving from inferior wealth.

2. Permissibility of displaying charity when it is safe from ostentation.

3. The virtue of secret charity and the greatness of its reward. In the authentic hadith: "...and a man who gave charity and concealed it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends," it is mentioned among the seven whom Allah will shade under the shadow of His Throne on a day when there is no shade but His.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 272–274:

Explanation of the words:

Hada-hum (guided them): guiding them to faith and righteous deeds.

Min khayr (of wealth): from wealth.

Fa-li-anfusikum (it is for your own selves): its immediate benefit is blessing and good repute, and its deferred benefit on the Day of Resurrection returns to yourselves.

Yuwaffa ilaykum (it will be repaid to you): its reward will be returned to you in full, without any reduction.

Uhsiru (they are confined): they were restrained and prevented from moving about freely because they had emigrated from their lands.

Darban fi al-ard (striving through the land): that is, journeying in it to seek provision through trade and other means, since the enemy had confined them.

Bi-simahum (by their marks): signs of their need, such as threadbare clothing and a pallid face.

Min al-ta'affuf (from restraint): refraining from asking people and abstaining from it.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 275–277:

Explanation of the words:

Ya'kuluna al-riba (يأكلون الربا): they take it and dispose of it by consuming it in their bellies, and by other means than eating. Riba here is riba al-nasi'a (the interest of deferment), and its reality is that a man owes you a debt; when its term falls due and he is unable to pay, you say to him: "Defer it and add [to it]," so you postpone it for a term and increase the principal by a specific amount. This is the riba of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic age), and it is practised today in the interest-based banks, which lend a person a sum until a term and add another amount, such as a tenth or more or less. Riba is forbidden by the Book, the Sunna and the consensus (ijma') of the scholars, whether it is riba al-fadl (the excess in exchange of like goods) or riba al-nasi'a.

La yaqumuna (لا يقومون): [they will not rise] from their graves on the Day of Resurrection.

Yatakhabbatuhu al-shaytan (يتخبطه الشيطان): the Shaytan strikes him irregularly.

Min al-mass (من المس): the mass is madness; it is said: "So-and-so has a mass of madness."

Mawi'idha (موعظة): a command or prohibition to abandon riba.

Fa-lahu ma salaf (فله ما سلف): it is not incumbent upon him to return the wealth that preceded his repentance.

Yamhaq Allahu al-riba (يمحق الله الربا): that is, He removes it little by little until nothing of it remains, like the waning of the moon at the end of the month.

Wa-yurbi al-sadaqat (ويربي الصدقات): He blesses the wealth from which it was given out, increases it, and multiplies its reward many times over.

Kaffarin athim (كفار أثيم): kaffar: one who is extremely disbelieving, who denies every truth, justice and good; athim: one immersed in sins, who leaves no major or minor sin without committing it.

The meaning of the two verses:

When Allah urged charity and promised for it a great reward and multiplied recompense, He mentioned the usurers who multiply their financial gains through riba, and by doing so they block the paths of righteousness and turn people away from the way of goodness. Instead of their wealth growing through charity, it grows through usury. So He, exalted is He, described their state when they rise from their graves: they rise, sit, stumble and fall, their condition being like that of one who is struck down in this world by the madness of possession, a sign by which they will be recognised on the Day of Resurrection, just as they are recognised by the swelling of their bellies, which are like a tent pitched before them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who consume riba will not rise except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch﴾. He, exalted is He, mentioned the cause of this punishment upon them, saying ﴿That﴾, that is, that disgrace and torment befell them, "because they said: 'Trade is only like riba,'" by rejecting Our judgment prohibiting riba and saying that sale is simply like riba, since riba is an increase at the end of the term while sale is at its beginning. Allah replied to them, saying: ﴿But Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba﴾. Since He has forbidden riba, there is no sense in objecting. They forgot that the increase in a sale is in the value of goods that rise and fall in price, and it proceeds according to the law of permission in commerce, whereas the increase at the end of a sale is merely an increase in time. Then He, exalted is He, said, explaining to His servants the path of salvation and warning against the way of destruction: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾, namely His prohibition of riba and His forbidding of it, and he desists, then ﴿he may keep what has passed﴾ before he knew of the prohibition, or before his repentance from it; and his affair is left to Allah. If He wills, He makes him steadfast in repentance and saves him; and if He wills, He forsakes him for the evil of his deeds and the corruption of his intention, and destroys him and casts him down. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But whoever returns [to riba] – those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾.

He, exalted is He, informed that by His justice He destroys riba, and by His bounty He increases charity, and that He does not love every ungrateful one who disobeys the law of Allah and His limits, every sinner who plunges into sins and commits transgressions. This was the meaning of the first verse [275]. As for the second verse [276], it is a true divine promise and a joyful glad tidings from Allah to everyone who believes, does righteous deeds, establishes the prayer in the manner in which it is to be established, and gives zakat, that they will have a complete reward with their Lord, which they will receive on the Day when they are in need of it in the gatherings of the Resurrection; and that they will not fear what lies ahead of them in this life and the Hereafter, nor will they grieve in this world or in the Hereafter.

Guidance from the two verses:

From the guidance of the two verses:

1- The explanation of the punishment of the one who consumes riba on the Day of Resurrection, for their considering riba permissible, their consuming it, and their failure to repent from it.

2- The prohibition of riba and of every forbidden wealth, because of the severe warning in the verse.

3- The attribute of love for Allah, exalted is He: He loves His friends, who are the people of faith in Him and obedience to Him, and He dislikes His enemies, who are the people of disbelief in Him and disobedience to Him, such as those who consume riba and other major sins.

4- The permissibility of sale, if it is concluded according to its conditions set out in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

5- Whoever repents of riba, his repentance is accepted, and what he gained from it before repentance is lawful for him, on a condition that will come in the verses after these.

6- The warning of Allah, exalted is He, of the destruction of riba and His promise of increasing charity.

7- The glad tidings of Allah, exalted is He, to the people of faith and righteous deeds, together with their establishing the prayer and giving zakat.

Guidance from the two verses:

From the guidance of the two verses:

1- The explanation of the punishment of the one who consumes riba on the Day of Resurrection, for their considering riba permissible, their consuming it, and their failure to repent from it.

2- The prohibition of riba and of every forbidden wealth, because of the severe warning in the verse.

3- The attribute of love for Allah, exalted is He: He loves His friends, who are the people of faith in Him and obedience to Him, and He dislikes His enemies, who are the people of disbelief in Him and disobedience to Him, such as those who consume riba and other major sins.

4- The permissibility of sale, if it is concluded according to its conditions set out in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

5- Whoever repents of riba, his repentance is accepted, and what he gained from it before repentance is lawful for him, on a condition that will come in the verses after these.

6- The warning of Allah, exalted is He, of the destruction of riba and His promise of increasing charity.

7- The glad tidings of Allah, exalted is He, to the people of faith and righteous deeds, together with their establishing the prayer and giving zakat.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 278–281:

Explanation of the words:

Ittaqu Allah (fear Allah): fear His punishment by obedience to Him, making obedience to Him a shield that protects you from His anger and punishment.

Wa dharu ma baqiya min al-riba (and leave what remains of usury): abandon whatever remains with you of usurious transactions.

Fa'dhanu bi harb (then be warned of war): know that there is war from Allah and His Messenger; take up your weapons, though no weapon will benefit you, for you are the defeated and the doomed.

Fa-lakum ru'us amwalikum (then you shall have your capital): after repentance, you have no claim except the principal that the debtor owes you; take it and leave the excess of usury.

Al-'usra (hardship): severe hardship and financial distress.

Fa-nazhratun ila maysarah (then let there be postponement until a time of ease): that is, waiting for the debtor until Allah eases matters for you, so that he repays you the capital you lent him.

Wa an tasaddaqu (and that you give charity): and that you give charity to the one in difficulty by forgoing what is owed to you, for that is better for you.

Meaning of the verses:

Occasioned by the mention of the punishment of those who consume usury in the preceding verses, Allah the Exalted addressed His believing servants, commanding them to fear Him, by obeying Him and abandoning His disobedience, and by giving up whatever usurious transactions remained with some of them, reminding them of their faith, since it is the nature of the believer to respond to the call of his Lord, to do what He commands and to abstain from what He forbids. So He said: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾. Then He threatened those who were slow to comply, saying: "But if you do not do so, then be warned of a harsh and fierce war from Allah and His Messenger." Then He explained to them the way of repentance and the path of escape from the trial and affliction of usury, saying: "But if you repent by abandoning usury, you shall have your capital, neither wronging nor being wronged by taking excess, nor being wronged by any reduction in your capital." If a debtor who owes you is in a state of hardship, it is obligatory to wait for him until he is in ease. And something else, which is better for you: that you give charity by forgoing all your debts, purifying your wealth which usury has touched and purifying your souls from its evil effects. Then Allah the Exalted reminded all His servants of the Day of Resurrection and its terrors and difficult standings, when the precise reckoning takes place and every soul, whether believing or disbelieving, righteous or wicked, is recompensed for what it earned of good and evil, and they are not wronged by any diminishing of their good deeds or any increase in their sins. So He said: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah; then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾. This instruction contained in this verse, numbered [280], is the last instruction that humanity received from its Lord, the Exalted, for this is the last thing sent down from heaven upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Guidance from the verses:

1- The obligation of repentance from usury and from all sins.

2- Whoever persists in usurious transactions, the ruler must fight him by restraining his hands until he gives up usury.

3- Whoever repents from usury is not wronged by taking from his capital; rather he is given it in full and complete, unless he gives charity by forgoing his usurious debts, which is better for him in state and outcome.

4- The obligation to remember the Hereafter and prepare for it through faith, righteous deeds, and abandoning usury and sins.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verse 282:

Explanation of the words:

tadayantum (you contract a debt): one of you gives credit to another in buying, selling, salam (advance purchase, pre-payment for goods to be delivered later) or loan.

ila ajalin musamman (for a specified term): a set time, in days, months or years.

bil-'adl (justly): without any addition or reduction, without deception or trickery, but in truth and fairness.

wa la ya'ba (let him not refuse): the one who knows how to write must not refuse to write.

wal-yumlil alladhi 'alayhi al-haqq (let the one who owes the debt dictate): because his dictation is an acknowledgement and affirmation of the right that is owed by him.

wa la yabkhas minhu shay'an (and let him not diminish anything of it): let him not reduce anything of the debt owed, even if it is small, such as a fils; and let him record all of it.

safihan aw da'ifan (foolish or weak): the safih is one who does not handle financial matters well; the da'if is one incapable of dictating, such as a mute person or a decrepit elderly man.

waliyyuhu (his guardian): the one who takes charge of his affairs and manages his interests because of his incapacity and deficiency.

min rijalikum (from among your men): that is, free Muslim men, excluding slaves and disbelievers.

an tadilla ihdahuma (that if one of them errs): forgets or makes a mistake due to her limited understanding.

wa la tas'amu (and do not be weary): do not become bored or tired of writing, even if the amount of the debt is small.

aqsatu 'inda Allah (more just in the sight of God): more upright in the judgment of God and His law.

wa aqwamu lil-shahadah (more steadfast for testimony): more firm for it and more conducive to establishing it, because writing is not forgotten, whereas testimony may be forgotten, or the witness may die or be absent.

wa adna alla tartabu (and more likely to prevent doubt): closer to ensuring that you do not doubt, unlike testimony without writing.

tudirunaha baynakum (you conduct it among yourselves): that is, you exchange it, the seller gives the goods and the buyer gives the money, so there is no need to write it down, and no sin or blame arises from it.

wa ashhidu idha tabaya'tum (and call witnesses when you conclude a sale): if one person sells a house, a garden or an animal to another, he should call witnesses to that sale.

wa la yudarra katibun wa la shahid (and let no scribe or witness be harmed): by being burdened with what he cannot bear, such as being summoned to bear witness in a distant place that is hard for him, or being asked to write falsely or to testify to something false.

fa-innahu fusuqun bikum (then it is indeed a transgression in you): that is, a departure from the obedience of your Lord; its sin will fall upon you and you will bear its consequence on the Day of Resurrection.

ittaqu Allah (fear God): in His commands, so carry them out, and in His prohibitions, so abstain from them. As He has taught you this, He will teach you everything you need; so praise Him with your tongues and thank Him with your deeds, and He will reward you for them, for He is All-Knowing of everything.

Meaning of the noble verse:

When God exhorted to charity, forbade usury, and called for pardon toward the insolvent debtor and for remitting the debt to him as charity, there might come to mind the notion that wealth has no importance or value in life. So this verse, the noble verse of debt, came to give wealth its due and raise its status, for it is the foundation of life. It established the obligation to preserve it, by writing down debts and calling witnesses to them, from those whose uprightness is accepted, and that the witnesses be two free Muslim men. If one of the two men is unavailable, two women stand in his place. God urged the one who knows how to write to write when he is able to do so, and forbade the witnesses, when called to give testimony, to shirk it. He also forbade the parties to a debt from failing to write down their debts, even if the debt is small and minor. God said: ﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, to its term﴾. Out of His mercy, God granted a dispensation not to write down a present trade in which the goods are delivered at the session and the price is received there, saying: {Except that it be present trade that you conduct among yourselves, for there is no blame on you that you not write it.} He commanded calling witnesses for sale, saying: ﴿And call witnesses when you conclude a sale...﴾ and forbade harming the scribe or the witness, by obliging the scribe to write when he is busy with his work, or the witness by requiring him to testify while he is likewise occupied, or by summoning him to distant places that burden him, since his role is voluntary, an act of good and nothing more. Then one should seek another scribe and another witness besides them if they are unable to do so due to their preoccupation. He warned against concealing testimony, against injustice and bias in writing, and against harming the scribe and the witness, saying: ﴿And if you do so, it is indeed a transgression in you...﴾ and emphasized this by commanding them to fear Him, saying: ﴿And fear God...﴾ by complying with His command and avoiding His prohibition, so that you may be perfected and attain happiness. And as He has taught you this beneficial knowledge, He continues to teach you, and He is All-Knowing of everything. This is the meaning of the noble verse: ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, then write it down...﴾

Guidance from the verse

From the guidance of the verse:

1- The obligation to write down debts, whether they arise from sale, purchase, salaf or loan. This is what Ibn Jarir affirmed, and he rejected the view that it is mere guidance or recommendation.

2- Observing the blessing by thanking for it, from God's words to the scribe: "as God has taught him, let him write," since He taught him writing and deprived others of it.

3- The permissibility of delegating dictation for one who is unable to dictate himself.

4- The obligation of justice and fairness in all matters, especially in writing down debts that are due and deferred.

5- The obligation to call witnesses to the writing, to strengthen it by this, and to avoid forgetting the amount of the debt and its term.

6- Witnesses to property must be no fewer than two just free Muslim men, and no others; and the two Muslim women whose testimony is prescribed stand in place of one man.

7- Eagerness to write down debts and resolve to do so, even if the debt is small and trivial.

8- The dispensation not to write down a present trade in goods and price exchanged between seller and buyer.

9- The obligation to call witnesses to the sale of real estate, farms and factories, and other matters of significance.

10- The prohibition of harming the scribe and the witness.

11- The fear of God causes knowledge and bestows understanding, by God's permission.

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 283–284:

Explanation of the words:

As-safar (the journey): going out of one's home and town openly, to a distance of four barids or more.

Wa lam tajidu katiban (and you do not find a scribe): one who would write for you; or you do not find the tools of writing, such as an inkwell and a pen.

Fa-rihanun maqbudah (then a pledge taken into possession): then substitute for the writing a pledge (rahn), whereby the debtor places a pledge with the creditor.

Fa-in amina ba'dukum ba'dan (and if one of you trusts another): then there is no need for a pledge.

Fa-l-yu'addi al-mu'taman amanatahu (let the one who is entrusted deliver his trust): that is, let him give back the debt he was entrusted with, where writing was impossible and his creditor did not take a pledge against his debt.

Athimun qalbuhu (his heart is sinful): because concealment is an act of the heart, so the sin is attributed to the heart.

Wa in tubdu (and if you reveal): if you make it manifest.

The meaning of the two verses:

When Allah, exalted is He, commanded witnessing and writing in sales, salam (advance sales) and loans in the preceding verses, He here commanded, when writing is impossible because there is no scribe or writing tools, and that is during travel, that a substitute for writing be taken in the form of a pledge, by which the debtor places a pledge with his creditor in place of writing, to secure his debt. This applies when there is no mutual trust and fear of default. As for when they trust one another, there is no harm in not taking a pledge. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession...﴾, and rihan is the plural of rahn. He said: ﴿And if one of you trusts another (and so you take no pledge), then let the one who is entrusted deliver his trust and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ in that matter. Then Allah, exalted is He, issued a firm prohibition to witnesses against concealing their testimony, saying: ﴿And do not conceal testimony...﴾, and He made clear the gravity of this sin, saying: ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is indeed sinful...﴾. And He informed that He knows what they do, and will recompense them according to His knowledge. This is a warning and threat from Him, glorified and exalted, to those who conceal testimony and those who speak falsehood in it. This is the meaning of the first verse [283]. As for the second verse [284], Allah, exalted is He, has informed that to Him belongs everything in the heavens and everything on the earth, in creation, ownership and disposal. Accordingly, whoever reveals what is in his self of good or evil, or conceals it, will be held to account for it. Then, after the reckoning, He forgives whom He wills among the people of faith and piety, and punishes whom He wills among the people of polytheism and disobedience. He has complete disposal, for all are His creation, His possession and His servants.

Guidance from the two verses:

1- Permissibility of taking a pledge while travelling and at home, as a means of securing a creditor's debt.

2- Permissibility of forgoing the pledge if there is assurance of repayment and no fear of default.

3- The prohibition of concealing testimony and speaking falsehood in it, and that this is among the greatest of major sins, as in the Sahih.

4- The servant is held to account for what he conceals in his self of doubt, polytheism, hypocrisy and other things, such as hatred of the friends of Allah and love of His enemies, and he is taken to task for them. Pardon is granted for the mere intention of a sin or wrongdoing, but not for doubt, polytheism, love or hatred from a sincere believer, based on the authentic hadith recorded by the six: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for me what my community whispers to themselves, so long as they do not speak or act upon it."

Commentary of al-Jaza'iri (Aysar al-Tafasir) on surah 2, verses 285–286:

Explanation of the words:

Āmana (believed): He affirmed with certainty the truth of the report, without ever wavering or doubting it.

Al-Rasūl (the Messenger): Our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

Kullun (each): Each of the Messenger and the believers.

Lā nufarriqu bayna aḥadin min rusulih (we make no distinction between any of His messengers): We believe in them all, and we are not like the Jews and Christians, who believe in some and disbelieve in others.

Samiʿnā (we hear): hearing with understanding, compliance and obedience.

Al-maṣīr (the final return): the place of return, i.e., our return to You, O our Lord, so forgive us.

Lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan (Allah does not burden a soul): Taklīf (burdening) means imposing upon someone what involves hardship and difficulty that can be borne.

Illā wus'ahā (except within its capacity): except what its capacity can bear and which is within its power.

Lahā mā kasabat (it shall have what it earned): of good.

Wa-ʿalayhā mā iktasabat (and it shall bear what it earned): of evil.

Lā tuʾākhidhnā (do not take us to account): do not punish us.

In nasīnā (if we forget): if we neglect what You have commanded us, or do what You have forbidden us, through forgetting, not deliberately.

Aw akhṭaʾnā (or err): we do other than what You commanded through error, without intending the act or resolving upon it.

Iṣran (a burden): a heavy obligation that weighs upon us and shackles us, holding us back from action.

Mawlānā (our Master): our Owner, our Lord and the one who manages our affairs; we have no protector other than You.

Meaning of the two verses:

It is reported that when the verse [2:284] was revealed, ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens...﴾, including ﴿...whether you show what is in yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it...﴾, the hearts of the believers were disturbed by it, and they said: "Who among us will be saved, if we are to be taken to account for what is hidden in our souls of concern, whisperings and inner thoughts?" So the Messenger (ﷺ) commanded them to be content with the judgment of Allah, the Exalted, and to submit to it, and said to them: "Say: We hear and we obey, and do not be like the Jews: ﴿They said: We hear and we disobey...﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:93]." When they said it sincerely, Allah the Exalted revealed these two verses: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers...﴾ He informed of their faith joined with the faith of their Prophet, honouring them and reassuring them, saying: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers. Each believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers. "We make no distinction between any of His messengers..."﴾ He then informed of their statement, which was the cause of Allah's response to them, saying of them: ﴿...And they say: We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.﴾ He, the Exalted, informed them that, out of His mercy towards them and the wisdom of His dealings with His creation, He does not burden any soul except within what its capacity can bear and what it is able to do; that it shall have what it earned of good, and be rewarded with good for it, and shall bear what it earned of evil, and be requited with evil for it, unless He pardons and forgives it. He said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It shall have what it has earned, and it shall bear what it has earned...﴾ He taught them how to call upon Him, so that He would say, "I have done it," as the report confirms, saying: "Say: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err. Our Lord, do not lay on us a burden like that You laid on those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Master, so give us victory over the disbelieving people.﴾" He indeed pardoned them for forgetting and error, lightened for them the legislation, and did not place upon them any hardship in the religion. He pardoned them, forgave them, showed them mercy, and gave them victory over the disbelievers, by proof and clarification, and in battles by the sword and the spear. So to Him belongs all praise and grace, and He is the Most High, the Exalted.

Guidance from the two verses:

1- Affirmation of the pillars of faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers.

2- The obligation to believe in all the messengers, and the prohibition of believing in some while rejecting others, which is disbelief, and Allah forbid.

3- The obligation to obey Allah and His Messenger, and to submit to and be content with what Allah and His Messenger have legislated, and the prohibition of rejecting any of it.

4- The lifting of hardship from this Ummah, as a mercy to it.

5- No accountability for forgetting or error: whoever forgets and eats or drinks while fasting bears no sin, or who errs and kills bears no sin.

6- Pardon for whispers of the soul, since the verse was revealed concerning it, so long as the believer does not speak or act upon them.

7- The teaching of this supplication and the recommendation of supplicating with it, following the example of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his Companions. It has been reported that whoever recites these two verses at night will be sufficed: ﴿The Messenger believes...﴾ to the end of the surah.
